speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over a relatively short period post-Independence, we transformed from a traditional, domestically focused economy to export-led industrialisation facilitated by multinational corporations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Subsequently, Singapore strategically pivoted towards developing modern services and made substantial investments in emerging sectors like biomedical industries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore also invests heavily in building up our infrastructure ahead of time so that when the wave arrives, we are ready to ride it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This forward-thinking approach, combined with the courage to explore uncharted territories, has proven successful, bolstered by a united and high-trust population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Going digital is a reality around the world and it is imperative for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we continue to transform and embrace the opportunities presented by digital transformation and immerse ourselves in the digital realm for our daily activities, we are confronted with a growing set of challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The digital landscape is becoming increasingly perilous, marked by the surge in online harms such as scams, ransomware, deep fakes, misinformation and other malicious cyber activities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Compounded by rapidly evolving tactics, the situation poses a constant challenge.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Much like cockroaches, scams often operate in the dark corners of the digital realm, exploiting vulnerabilities and thriving in unsuspecting spaces.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are agile, quick to evolve and adept at camouflaging themselves, making it challenging to eradicate them entirely.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, just as we believe that we figured out the latest scamming trick, new and more sophisticated threats emerge.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Notably, a global study reveals that Singapore, unfortunately, bears a significant brunt, with scam victims in the country experiencing an average loss of US$4,031 per individual.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This could be a substantial loss of hard-earned savings for some Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In MacPherson, I have encountered several residents who were victims of scams.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In late 2021, one young resident, Ms Tan, shared about how she and others lost money to fraudulent transactions on her credit card when she did not receive or provide to anyone her one-time password (OTP).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Quoting her, "Even without evidence that the consumers have received the OTP sent by the banks, that is, through a history of incoming message from the telco, banks requested customers to make payment for the fraudulent transactions without investigating whether the OTPs could have been diverted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Frustrated by their disadvantageous position in dispute against banks, consumers oftentimes bear the burden of making up to five-figure payments for these transactions." As an ordinary citizen and consumer, it is typically difficult to retrieve information or history of SMSes from the telecommunications company (telco) and the victim usually finds themselves to and fro between the bank, telco, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Police.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In another example, I met my elderly resident, Mr Yee, who fell prey online to an investment scheme supposedly endorsed by then Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He did not understand how credit card transactions work online and consequently was charged several thousand dollars in fraudulent credit card bills, which he could ill-afford as he only had a few hundred dollars left in his savings account.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He was under tremendous stress as he was frail and worried that he will lose everything.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We managed to get the bank to waive it, given his dire circumstances, but how many such goodwill write-offs are possible?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are just some of the notable cases that I have come across in MacPherson and I am certain my Parliamentary colleagues have many similar examples as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such cases are compelling motivation for us to move this Motion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, the escalating global artificial intelligence (AI) arms race raises concerns about potential compromises on ethical considerations as powerful technology companies prioritise winning at all costs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This heightened competition may lead to a disregard for addressing social disparities, including the widening gap between the digitally know-how and the digitally know-nots, exacerbating divisions within the population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Additionally, if institutions solely concentrate on leveraging AI or any emerging technology for enhanced productivity without concurrently investing in workforce training and re-training initiatives, ordinary citizens could grow fearful of what we will lose more than being hopeful of what we can gain from technological advancements as a society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This fear, in turn, can impede Singapore's progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The trustworthiness of critical infrastructures and essential services also plays a role in shaping public confidence towards the security of their personal data.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With 99% of resident households in Singapore connected to the Internet, we have one of the highest internet penetration rates in the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is testament to Singapore's progress, but it also means that we are all the more susceptible to online threats.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: DBS' repeated digital service disruptions in 2023, Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings lost to Android malware scams and personal data breaches in public healthcare – these incidents affected a significant portion of our population and in turn, affect the public's trust in the digital.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These issues, if left to fester, will undermine trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Not being able to trust every information received, every transaction made, every voice heard and every image seen is paralysing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Trust is fundamental in a society as there will inevitably be difficult times when individuals need to be willing to temporarily sacrifice individual interests in favour of collective societal benefits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Trust is important for value-creating transactions to happen, for creative ideas to be shared and not be suppressed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, if we do not make a clear stand and actively manage these issues, we risk losing the public's trust in the digital world, thereby losing out on the benefits of convenience to citizens and benefits of productivity and innovation for our national economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the onset of this speech, I have explained the context for why we have moved this Motion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have also emphasised why trust is important and strengthening trust in a digital society must be the end goal of this Motion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Allow me to elaborate on the "safe" and "inclusive" tenets of this Motion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Underlying a safe online environment are: number one, trust in digital transactions First, we need reliable digital infrastructure so as to provide the foundation for secure, reliable and accessible digital services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Unreliable systems, frequent outages or vulnerabilities in the infrastructure make users skeptical about the security of their transactions, hindering the growth of digital trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thus, the organisations across all sectors must intentionally and systematically incorporate measures and practices that prioritise and enhance trust throughout the entire digital transaction process.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Scams erode trust by exploiting unsuspecting users, leading to financial losses and undermining confidence in digital transactions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Cybersecurity threats, such as data breaches and identity theft via malwares, contribute to fear and suspicion among users.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Privacy breaches and unauthorised access to personal information can also make individuals hesitant to engage in digital activities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must ensure that related policies and capabilities continually evolve to keep up with the rampant and fast-changing threats online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Online harms, including cyberbullying and harassment, have real-life consequences on individuals' mental health and well-being, hampering their potential.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Further, vulnerable groups, such as children and the elderly, are particularly susceptible to online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must promote respectful and responsible behaviours and implement measures that protect vulnerable groups from exploitation, thereby fostering trust among users of all demographics.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The interconnectedness of online and physical worlds often influence real-life relationships.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should focus on creating more positive online experiences so that human connections remain meaningful even as we go digital.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ultimately, people will be keener to participate if they feel safe.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must create a safe online space that allows broad-based participation if we are to achieve a truly inclusive digital society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In short, a safe online environment is a cornerstone of building trust in a digital society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This trust, in turn, contributes to the growth and success of the digital ecosystem, positively impacting both online and offline aspects of individuals' lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Key to this include: number one, access to essential services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As essential services such as Government, healthcare, finance and telco services increasingly transition to digital platforms, these must remain accessible to everyone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Number two, digital skills empowerment and closing social gaps.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must empower our citizens with digital access and the right skills for active participation in the digital society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must be mindful of not creating new gaps between the digitally savvy and those who are not.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By doing so, individuals, including the vulnerable, can gain the confidence to navigate digital platforms, reducing the digital divide and fostering trust in their ability to engage with digital technologies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must evolve jobs and workplaces to keep up with the fast-changing digital landscape, whilst ensuring the workforce continues to have the right skill sets, so that everyone can contribute meaningfully, regardless of age or background.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must ensure that digital platforms and environments are safe, kind and respectful as I have had earlier articulated, so that citizens are not denied their voice or meaningful online participation for fear of being "cancelled" just because one holds a different view from a vocal few.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must ensure digital interfaces are inclusive by design so that citizens of all ages, languages and physical conditions can comfortably and confidently engage in the digital space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I will first cover five calls to action, while my fellow GPC members and PAP MPs will speak in greater depth on the rest.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Companies, given the competitive nature, are fundamentally unwilling to cooperate and share information and best practices, which could help with timely interventions or enforcement against scams or digital threats.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ironically, collaboration on this front would have catalysed learning and improvements to their operations and business.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, companies tend to be more willing to share data and experiences with the Government, which could then anonymise and aggregate such information.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we need a stronger framework for public and private players to share information on scams, to enable faster detection and intervention.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Taking a leaf from the "Stop Scams UK" that allows industry players to share intelligence and collaborate on scam-related initiatives, our Government can and should take the lead in setting up a similar information-sharing mechanism with the industry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleague Vikram Nair will also touch on this in his speech later.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, Government to further integrate expertise and prioritise resources to regulate and enforce online safety.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Singapore Government has done much to combat scams and online harms, from legislation updates, introduction of codes to introducing new tools for companies' and public's use.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is also encouraging to note the establishment of Anti-Scam Command in 2022 and co-location of major banks' staff with the Police to facilitate scam detection and reporting.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the broader efforts in combatting scams and online harms still necessitate extensive coordination across various Government agencies and departments, and private institutions, such as banks and telcos, which may have varying mandates and resource priorities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, there is scope for further integration of expertise and resource prioritisation in regulating and enforcing online safety.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleague Yip Hon Weng will further touch on this and specifically on stakeholder coordination later in his speech.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, device manufacturers and digital service providers to strengthen safeguards against malware and ensure their offerings are safe by design and default.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have seen an increase in prevalence of scams enabled by malware on users' mobile devices.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These malware threats are difficult for everyday citizens to detect.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even with public education, it will be difficult for individuals to know if their phones and devices have been compromised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even someone who is in the tech industry will find it difficult to know.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, device manufacturers and digital service providers should be proactive in informing consumers of vulnerabilities detected and in strengthening their safeguards against malware to ensure that their offerings are safe by design and default.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From another perspective, greater transparency and evident efforts in enhancing safe use will bolster customer confidence and drive sales.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many digital service providers continue to use authentication methods, such as traditional passwords that are vulnerable to phishing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As bad actors evolve their methods, banks and e-commerce platforms with their powerful tech capabilities have a responsibility in keeping their customers' accounts secure and should thus be adopting phishing-resistant authentication, such as FIDO passkeys.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fifth, everyone can play their part in making Singapore's digital society safe, gracious and inclusive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we spend more time online, the digital and physical worlds are converging and our actions in either realm can have a profound impact on the other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ultimately, we should ask ourselves what kind of environment do we desire to see in the digital world?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we desire safety, inclusiveness, kindness and respect in the real world, we should also aspire to create the same online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Why should the digital world be any different from the real one?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleague Vikram Nair will also speak on this later.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As my hon colleagues engage in deeper discussions on online harms later in their speeches, I wish to highlight the need to ensure a safe space for freedom of ideas and expression online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Internet has the power to amplify the voices of a vocal few.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If this ability becomes misguided, it risks drowning out or cancelling others who hold a different opinion or who are, simply, different.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, this call of action calls on every one of us to continue upholding the values of kindness and respect online and offline, to look beyond ourselves and reach out to others who may be in need of help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Following my opening speech, the remaining speeches by our PAP MPs will focus on the remaining eight calls of actions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleagues Nadia Samdin, Wan Rizal and Mariam Jaafar will be covering this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Next, reviewing the approach to victims of scams by unauthorised transactions, with larger players doing more to prevent losses and share consequences.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleagues Hany Soh and Yip Hon Weng will also be covering this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleague, Nadia Samdin will be speaking on this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleague Nadia Samdin will also be covering this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My colleagues Jessica Tan, Nadia Samdin and Yip Hon Weng will be speaking on this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Driving corporates and community organisations to promote awareness of essential digital skills and partner public sector to help close digital skill gaps.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleagues Jessica Tan, Hany Soh, Sharael Taha and Mariam Jaafar will be speaking on this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Driving stronger partnerships between public, private and individuals to deepen focus on educating our young and old on digital literacy, scams and online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleagues Darryl David, Wan Rizal, Sharael Taha and Yip Hon Weng will be speaking on this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And finally, strengthening efforts in establishing future-ready workplaces for a more digitally-savvy workforce.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My hon colleague Sharael Taha will also be speaking on this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Since Independence, Singapore has always been fearless in breaking through the status quo, and daring to transform and reform over the relatively few decades.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our country has evolved from a traditional economy primarily focused on domestic sectors to an export-oriented industrialisation driven by multinational corporations (MNCs) and then to the development of modern service industries and investment emerging sector to maintain our competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore has also made forward-looking investments in infrastructure development, enabling it to seize opportunities as they arise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Coupled with unity, high trust and cooperation of its people, Singapore has been able to reach where it is today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, the increasing opportunities brought about by a digital transformation, we have also faced increasingly severe challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Cyber threats, such as scams, ransomware, deep fakes and misinformation are rapidly on the rise, significantly increasing the risks in the digital environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the saying goes, the higher the level, the greater the devil.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These cyber threats are like cockroaches that will never say die.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, the escalating global competition in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) has raised concerns about potential ethical compromises.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Powerful technology companies may prioritise winning the competition at all costs and this potentially leads neglecting social disparities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Additionally, the credibility of critical infrastructure and essential services can also affect the public's confidence in their personal data security.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If left unchecked, these issues will erode trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: People will not be able to trust every piece of information they receive, every transaction they conduct, every voice heard and every image seen.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, there are no absolutes in the world and in the real world, nothing is perfect.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In real life, we do not refrain from leaving our homes for fear of encountering accidents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, trust is a key factor in building the foundation of society as difficulties are inevitable in life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During these times, we may need to temporarily sacrifice personal interest in exchange for the collective interests of society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Trust is also important in conducting transactions that create value and sharing ideas.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, if we do not clearly set our position and actively address these issues, we may lose trust in the public in the area of digital technology, resulting in the loss of convenience for the people, as well as productivity and innovation benefits for our economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We may not be able to totally stamp out such risks or threats as they are like cockroaches.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But if we can do more, if everyone is willing to take on a larger share of the responsibility, we can protect more people and reduce the harms or damage to the ordinary citizen.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As Singapore continues to advance towards a digital society, public and private stakeholders must collaborate as a whole-of-nation to manage the risks, address the challenges and help each other thrive in the digital future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On restoring trust, I will touch on scams and AI.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I read with interest about an interview given by Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) Minister Josephine Teo to Lianhe Zaobao in December on MCI's priorities for this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Among other things, she underscored the urgent and pressing need to restore confidence in the digital space and telecommunications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To block 300 million calls is a staggering statistic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But I would surmise that many other scam calls would have gotten through.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our parents, residents and we ourselves are all in the pool of potential victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since I spoke this House in mid-September on scam losses and doing right by bank customers, the landscape has evolved further.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that banks appear to be taking more steps to prevent scams and to stop scams in progress.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I cannot over-emphasise why banks of all people need to do this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Banks are making healthy profits and have the resources and expertise to do more to protect and detect scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, the modus operandi of scammers has continued to evolve and leverage on victim psyche.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From impersonating Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and bank officers, they now impersonate officers from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Phishing scams involving Paylah! have been effective in spoofing SMS messages typically sent by DBS Bank.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On New Year's Day this year, I, too, received the SMS about the withdrawal of $289 from my Paylah! account and a link to stop the transaction if it was unauthorised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I was in the midst of some work then, I did not scrutinise the message carefully and clicked on the link to stop the transaction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The link then brought me to a page to enter my banking credentials, whereupon I had my Eureka moment and stopped in my tracks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Not so fortunate were some residents who received the same SMS who then came to the Meet-the-People Session (MPS) in desperation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All in all, I have to conclude that these organised criminals must have very good consultants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even modes of savings we thought were very safe, like our Central Provident Fund (CPF) monies and fixed deposits, are not safe against scams and malware.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is leading to a change in thinking about digital transactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But from a helicopter perspective, "money lock" is actually a concession that the digital space is not that safe.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would not like to exaggerate the situation but I would say that we are moving towards a crisis of confidence in digital banking, without stronger intervention by Government regulators.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, customers need to do their part.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Customers need to be wary and alert to prevent being scammed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, we should be ever mindful not to expect too much from the public.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As stated in a Straits Times Forum page letter on 22 September, it is not always possible for people to be on full alert against scams as one's level of alertness could be affected by multi-tasking, stress, fatigue or medication.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ninety-nine percent were worried about becoming victims of scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These numbers show that the threat of scams is very real and that more needs to be done.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The MAS has been working on further regulating banks and more must be done on prevention and loss sharing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken on this previously and shall not repeat myself today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have also made a submission to the MAS on the risk-sharing framework for scam losses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the last few months, I have received skeptical feedback from some members of the public that the banks' interests will always be protected at the expense of the customer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope that the MAS will demonstrate that this is not true.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the more general issue of digital communications and services, I acknowledge the potential of the Online Criminal Harms Act (OCHA) to prevent scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Among other powers, the OCHA will enable law enforcement to proactively issue orders such as access blocking directions and app removal directions to require internet service providers to protect the public from scams and other malicious cyber activity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On OCHA, it would be good to know when all the provisions will be effective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, I note the announcement by the Minister for Communications and Information on the setting up of a multi-agency group called the Task Force on Resilience and Security of Digital Infrastructure and Services – what I call the RSD task force.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The work of the RSD task force is set to oversee matters of public confidence in the country's digital services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since banking is such a big part of digital infrastructure and services, should MAS not be on the task force?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Twenty twenty three is generally hailed as the year when ChatGPT came into the world's consciousness and everyone started exploring its potential.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The focus is now shifting to how AI tools can be deployed at scale as AI develops in sophistication.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From asking AI to carry out a specific task, AI tools have gone from classification AI to generative AI where content is created, like mimicking voices of loved ones.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has further developed into interactive AI where AI tools can interact with humans to reason and arrive at watershed decisions affecting work and personal lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Last year, the Government published Singapore's National AI Strategy 2.0.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In it, the report acknowledged both the vast potential of AI to do both good and bad.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The bad aspects included how AI could amplify harms such as enabling scams using deepfakes, spreading this information and others.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should be acutely aware of AI's pitfalls and the need for AI regulation to ensure that Singaporeans remain safe online.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has set up the AI Verify Foundation, which published a discussion paper last year entitled, "Generative AI: Implications for Trust and Governance".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The paper was stated to be targeted at senior leaders in Government and business, advocating for more discourse and collaboration on building an ecosystem for the trusted and responsible adoption of generative AI.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Among the emergent risks of generative AI listed by the paper were the making of mistakes, copyright infringements and the spreading of toxicity and cyber threats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Apart from these emergent risks, the fact that AI will lead to drop losses and disinformation alone will erode public trust in the digital arena.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Across the world, the fundamental question of whether human beings really want to go further with AI is being asked.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is growing concern about creating more powerful AI tools that may replace the human function and even control human interactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The concern comes from those in the AI industry as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, there is a non-profit organisation based in the United States (US) called the Future of Life Institute.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Its multidisciplinary international team engages in policy work aimed at improving AI governance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of the big questions identified for reflection include the following questions: (a) whether we should let machines flood our information channels with possible propaganda and untruth; (b) whether we should automate away all jobs including, the fulfilling ones; and (c) whether we should develop non-human minds that might eventually outnumber, outsmart and replace us.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Other prominent thinkers have cautioned that reliance on AI tools to process information and to think may result in the potential loss of human reasoning and analytical ability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaking for myself, I must say that the thought of major decision-making in the world being outsourced to AI tools is simply unacceptable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, the need to harness AI and yet ensure humans are in charge will be the big challenge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Technology should be our servants and not our masters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should take time to reflect on what is happening and not let technology run away unbridled with us in toll.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My speech today was on restoring trust in the digital arena.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have highlighted that online scams and the risk of AI have put trust under a microscope.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Motion today posits that a whole-of-nation approach should be taken to sustain trust by building an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am able to support the Motion as I agree that everyone has a role to play.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, for the reasons I have stated, my view is that it is incumbent upon the Government and businesses to spearhead this effort.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak today about the consumer protection angle to scams and secondly, more broadly, on the landscape in the age of AI and Singapore's survivability.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is, I would say, agreement on all sides of the House that it is a serious issue, especially in the era of digital banking, where senior citizens who grew up in a world of face-to-face counter transactions now can have their bank accounts and life savings depleted at the click of the device by a scammer far away, outside of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is a serious issue, especially in societies such as Singapore, where we progressed rapidly from third world to first and seniors growing up in the pre-digital era today exist in a world of digital access and digital technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is the first point about consumer protection.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In recent times, there have been efforts by the MAS – initially called the risk sharing framework or risk allocation framework, depending on how commentators look at it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But the key point has to be this: the norms that we approach consumer safety in banking, the approach to consumer safety for banking should not be too different from consumer safety in other more tangible areas of the marketplace.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I shared to the Minister of State from MAS not too long ago, if today, a company had a consumer product and if somebody could be tricked by a stranger into configuring that product wrongly so that there was either bodily harm or damage to property resulting in the loss of someone's entire life savings, we know what the consumer protection approach would be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see that with vehicles, where if there is a design flow in the vehicle that predisposes to human error or catastrophic outcomes of human error, that vehicle has to recall, that manufacturer is dealt with in a very serious way.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, again, we see quite a different situation between these consumer products.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Once again, I call upon this Government to take a consumer protection focus and make sure that manufacturers as well as service providers, including financial institutions, are held accountable in a way that is not too different from other sectors of society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If your family owns a car and there is a design issue leading to bodily harm or loss of your life savings, you know what the manufacturer must do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, that is the first part of my speech, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The second part of my speech will be on the age of AI and what Singapore needs to do to adapt.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I spoke on this last year, during the debate on the President's Address.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Early last year, I spoke on the age of AI and it was a humbling moment, because after the speech was delivered and it got a little bit of viral traction online, I think, just a little bit over 100,000 people around the world watched it – not that many.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we started getting emails, messages, from people around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Someone from the USA wrote to me, someone from Africa wrote in as well and it touched a chord.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is about what Singapore represents to the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When people see our Parliamentarians, whether our Ministers, office holders, whether our backbenchers of various persuasions, looking to the future about what the world will be like, people look at what Singapore is thinking about and they want us to try and find the way forward as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, on the issue of AI and the issue of deepfakes, I have a few suggestions as well for the Government to consider.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some I have put forward before in Parliamentary Questions and in my speeches, but let me just reiterate again.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: No government, regardless of which political party they come from, will be able to govern in any country without that fundamental basis for deliberative, democratic discussion.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That means, as a society, we need to deal with this pre-emptively.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Prime Minister not too long ago, in a Facebook post, talked about how there was a deepfake of him trying to sell certain investment products, a fake video.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Project that forward three, five years, 10 years, with more computing power, you can imagine how authentic those deepfakes are going to be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also need to continue moving upstream, a point which I made to the Education Minister yesterday in Question Time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: From young, we will have to continue training and teaching and bringing up our young Singaporeans, our children and grandchildren, to be even more aware of deepfakes and how subtle they can be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, as a young Clementi friend not too long ago, this young Clementi friend was sharing about his worry about deepfakes, saying, "You know, look, some of these look a bit sus", suspicious.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But the whole point is, the first step is to have that healthy scepticism to sense when something might be a bit "sus".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we need to move on this very quickly because by the time the genie is completely out of the bottle, the horse has bolted, it is much harder to rebuild these norms and reconstruct the democratic process in our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, in summary, Mr Speaker, just two key points, but fundamentally about seeing through the eyes of our people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The first, seeing through the eyes of our consumers and making sure that firms in the digital space and in the financial sector, retail banking services, they treat consumer protection the same way online as we would treat consumer protection for an offline tangible product in the home, around the home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There has been mention of the AI roadmap version 2.0, but sometimes let us also ask ourselves, can we have even higher levels of ambition?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: From public domain information, if I recall correctly, not too long ago, I think less than a decade ago, Microsoft pumped $1 billion investment into OpenAI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It seemed like a big amount then, but in hindsight, it seems like it was a quite a good deal at the time, given what OpenAI grew into.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This also links to a point I made a few years back during a Budget debate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes when we invest ahead of the market, invest in certain technological capabilities which may see tenuous today, but which could have high yields tomorrow, it means that we are able to get those dividends later on.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many of the big tech firms today, whether Apple, Google, Meta, back then known as Facebook, would not have seemed sure bet investments in their very early years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But those who were willing to make those bets yielded substantial dividends and today our tech powerhouses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, let us think about that as we move into the next phase of AI, the next phase of tech in the digital world for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I stand in support of the Motion by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These changes have enabled ease and speed of access, ability to connect or interact, bringing benefits as well as new capabilities and opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we saw during the COVID-19 pandemic, digital connectivity enabled people to continue to access timely information, services and to communicate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses and work could continue – albeit virtually.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Increasingly, access to many services for living are digital.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From everyday tasks such as booking a taxi or private hire car, ordering food or making a restaurant reservation, making payments, getting information or directions, to accessing and transacting Government services and banking transactions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Even to get discounts requires you to scan a QR code or go online.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For some organisations, job applications and interviews are done online.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The latest news is availably digitally as soon as it happens or even as it happens.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If an individual is digitally excluded, he or she will not get timely information, services and its benefits.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is therefore important to ensure that no one is left behind as we become increasingly digital.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore takes a digital first but not digital-only approach as a central organising principle to harness the innovation potential and productivity but still ensuring that those who may not be comfortable with using digital technologies not be excluded from essential services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But while we continue to provide non-digital options, we must work to encourage and enable as many as possible to participate digitally.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we do not, what it will mean in a digital first but not digital only society is that those who do not use digital will miss out on the ease, timeliness and benefits that digital can offer.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Let us just take a simple example of the collection of the Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers to illustrate the point.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You can get the physical CDC vouchers by going to a community club (CC).

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To do so, you will be required to make time to go to the CC when it is open.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If you are lucky, there is no queue and you do not have to wait in line to get you CDC vouchers at the CC before you can use them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If instead you "collect" your CDC vouchers online using your Singpass, it would take you a minute or even less and you can proceed to use your CDC vouchers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The point applies to many other transactions that we do like banking.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You can go to the bank to get your transactions done which requires travel and time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It also has to be done during the opening hours of the bank.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With online banking, you can do so anytime, from wherever you are.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This now brings me to the critical point of digital safety and resilience which impacts trust and adoption.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You heard from all the previous speakers about the concerns, the risks, the dangers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I would like to just make a few points on this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It must be accompanied with the ability to use digital technologies effectively and safely and trust in the security and resilience of the digital environment and the platform in order for someone to really benefit from it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This includes important skills to stay safe online such as how to interact safely, how to protect your personal privacy online and how to effectively search for and discern information.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The increasing use of new technologies does have its risks and safeguards against cyber risks, scams and misinformation is vital to increase building confidence and trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While there are measures including legislation that have been introduced to safeguard the online space from harmful content and Government agencies continue to implement strategies with critical services and digital platform providers to prevent, detect and recover monies lost to scammers, more still needs to be done to secure digital transactions and online transactions and protect vulnerable users.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When we think of vulnerable users, we tend to think of seniors and those less digitally savvy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Sadly, I have had both seniors who lost their life savings to scams as well as younger individuals who had been scammed, approach me for assistance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Recently, a young resident in her 20s came to see me for help as she had worked hard to save her money, and had spent a few years building up her savings, but as a result of an online transaction she made, unfortunately she lost all her savings.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To add to it, she had her bank account details and credit card credentials stolen which resulted in unauthorised credit card payments as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as we talk about the dangers and risks, there are also opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we put more demands on all the larger players, and the key players and stakeholders, I will say that there is also an opportunity for platform and service players in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore is an advanced market with high levels of connectivity, as I have shared earlier, and also high levels of residents owning smartphones.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This provides platform and service players an opportunity to use Singapore as a base for innovation to apply and showcase higher standards of security.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do urge all players to do this, because as the Government pushes the measures, if all players come together, it will be a great opportunity for us to try new things, as Dr Tan Wu Meng had said, to really make Singapore that showcase to bring trust and confidence back in the digital space.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But what we now need to do is to manage that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, let me now also talk about the role of users and public education.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Industry players and Government play a big role to strengthen digital safety and security and digital literacy of persons using these applications and online systems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Public education and efforts to equip people with digital literacy, especially for certain segments like seniors and vulnerable segments, have been effective and have helped adoption.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But more needs to be done and more efforts need to be continual because the digital space does not stay static.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But, I do want to make a point about each of us and the role that we have to play.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We do need to remind ourselves that what we do to protect ourselves in our physical interactions should also be practised digitally.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Take, for example, in our physical lives, before we let someone enter our homes, we would check on who they are and we would not let anyone suspicious or someone we do not know into our homes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We would not give our NRIC details, bank account information or ATM card to anyone we do not know or trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These same principles and practices must be applied when we are online and using our digital devices and applications.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Otherwise, no matter what measures and legislation are in place to improve digital safety and security, they would not be able to protect us in our digital transactions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, we all have to do our part.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While digital literacy allows us to transact digitally, one of the areas when people do hit issues with transaction is the ability to get help to resolve these issues can, sometimes, be quite challenging, given how access to support is currently structured.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Unless you are a victim of fraud or have been scammed, most helpline numbers provided take quite a bit of navigation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Prioritising support for those who have been scammed is necessary.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, users of digital services when faced with issues during their transaction, do also need support to resolve their transaction issues.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do agree that it is challenging to resource support given manpower constraints, cost and capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as commercial businesses and Government services become more digital-first, we need to rethink the model of support and find more effective ways to provide timely access to support for users when they encounter issues with their digital transactions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will reassure and build digital trust and confidence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Especially when transactions involve monies, it can cause anxiety for users, young or old.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do want to touch on another point about digital inclusion and that is about the ability to participate in opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: New areas of technologies, including AI, have the potential to enable new capabilities, cause disruptions, of course, but create new ways of doing things and generating new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore continues to have ambitious plans to leverage new technologies to grow and bring benefits to our people and businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But it will require new governance models as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, my point is, to realise these ambitious plans, we will need people with skillsets in new areas of technology and cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is to build thoughtful design and solutions to really benefit from these new technologies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What it also means is good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But in order to take advantage of these opportunities will require new skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Organisations must make investments to support their employees in building new skillsets, educational institutions must prepare our students and those in the workforce for these opportunities, individuals of all ages and career stages must be open to learning and taking on new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There must be investments by the Government and the private sector to build deep skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: New technologies will allow for new ways of doing things and this involves more than technologies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And this brings me to a point about a diverse workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we discuss building an inclusive and safe digital society, core to our Motion is our People.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not about being a digitally advanced society with the best infrastructure, policies and skills or level of excellence and technology adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The official press release describing the framework states that, and I quote, "All parties have responsibilities to be vigilant and to take precautions against scams." Financial institutions need to implement robust controls to safeguard customer accounts and to detect and clamp down on suspicious transactions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Customers need to take precautions to not frivolously release their banking credentials and to practise cyber hygiene.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Losses would then be assigned according to how far each party falls short of these responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, in practice, fraud is almost always perpetrated on the weaker link in the chain, in this case, the vulnerable consumer, more often than not, than on the relatively better-equipped and technologically sophisticated bank or telecoms company.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, the equitable sharing framework becomes less about fairly distributing losses, but about distributing responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Losses, when they occur, would appear overwhelmingly borne by the consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, we should only expect the framework to yield equitable outcomes if the fair assignment of responsibilities were all that mattered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Anyone who has bargained over the price of fish or vegetables at the market or negotiated a salary or a raise with an employer or taken part in discussions over the distribution of chores or workload would know full well how power differentials matter massively and how the altar, how the pie ends up being split.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A large literature on the theory of bargaining shows that those in possession of power, tend to do better in negotiations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In cases where the bargaining is explicitly antagonistic, canonical models suggest that those who are more patient and are able to make the first move possess an advantage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even when we allow for the possibility that players see the benefits of cooperation and embed this in their negotiations, the outcome remains heavily conditioned by each party's relative bargaining power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, those who are better able to walk away tend to do better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we look carefully at the two parties involved in negotiating a settlement over fraudulent claims, it is clear who has the greater power, patience and ability to hold firm to their offer, and that is the bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If they can simply demonstrate that they have not erred in effecting a fraudulent transfer, they can currently credibly insist on refusing any share of the loss altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And write-offs, when they do occur, are typically only a small fraction of the institution's balance sheet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In stark contrast, scams are often ruinous for the depositor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the extreme, they could constitute either an individual's entire life savings, or worse, it could saddle an unwitting "mule" with onerous debt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is the split then that best reflects distributive justice?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, the notion of a 50/50 split should not be seen as one where each party takes an equal nominal share.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, the notion of an equal split suggests that each is made to bear a burden that is commensurate with what they are able to afford.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is why the Government needs to step in to empower depositors with a more robust set of laws that offer financial protection to consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I had previously raised this point in a speech on the Financial Services and Markets Bill delivered last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, I will elaborate why doing so will not only help redress the power imbalance between customers and banks, but also why it is fundamentally fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It explained closer to the end of that year that it was taking longer than expected and the release was further postponed in the middle of last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MAS finally published a joint consultation paper in October, but it was extremely circumscribed to deal only with phishing scams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alas, this approach will absolve financial institutions and communications companies from the costs of business, so long as they have done their part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this does not close the door to other resolution mechanisms, such as the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre (FIDReC), it remains too cavalier in apportioning liability in the first instance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: SRF is a split based on effort, not outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, should there be a realised loss, as long as the financial institution or telecom operator can demonstrate that they have satisfied a certain set of obligations – which, to be honest, is not even exhaustive – their loss share will not be half.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It would not be a third or even a quarter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Imagine that there are two cars driving side-by-side on the road.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is the responsibility of both drivers not to drive beyond the speed limit and to stay in their lanes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Should one car brake suddenly and it is ahead, the following car should always maintain a safe distance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what if the cars were side-by-side and a child were to run out in front of one of them?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If one of them were to swerve to avoid an accident and the other fails to yield, it is hard to say that only one of the cars should bear responsibility for the crash.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Financial fraud, while preventable to a certain extent with sound system design and due diligence, is almost certainly likely to occur, regardless of the best efforts of either party.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Much like the analogy that I just shared, there will seldom be clear-cut pinning of blame on one party versus another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, it is only fair that both sides bear some of the costs of the loss.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a legislative may, of course, seem foolhardy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The standard line trod out by critics is that protecting customers from the consequences of scams must mean that they are less likely to take the necessary precautions to safeguard against falling for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is what is often referred to as moral hazard – since one side is protected, one takes less care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But while I am sympathetic to the argument in principle, a crude application of this theory is problematic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, this kind of argument places too little faith in the agency of Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, why would anyone wish to fall victim to a scam?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if they bore only limited consequences, most of us would take active steps to counteract crime, even when we do not receive a clear pay-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should not think that only a catastrophic loss would be sufficient for individuals to practise the necessary amount of cyber hygiene.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nobody would rather lose $100 to a scammer, rather than none, if they can avoid it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, this opens up the possibility that unscrupulous scammers may use this very notion of victim protection to defraud banks directly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, this is true for any form of insurance fraud and there are well-established mechanisms for identifying and clamping down on such abuse, which would emerge when losses are more equally apportioned to both sides.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That naturally brings me to the sort of indirect long-run benefits to having a system where both sides are made to bear some of the losses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a law would also likely lead to a sequence of favourable developments in the financial ecosystem that could render it more robust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Financial institutions would take more care to police phishing and fraud.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since they can no longer pass on most of the costs of losses to consumers, there would also be more pressing incentive to chase down transfers made to suspicious counterparties and they would no longer condone unauthorised purchases made with ill-gotten money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Fraud detection and prevention tools have been around for a long time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the widespread rollout of generative artificial intelligence has made the rapid deployment of the latest algorithms both less costly and simultaneously more sophisticated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Merchants and banks, in turn, would apply more caution as they seek to implement their own safeguards lest they lose the right to accept payments or transfers electronically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Insurance schemes to cover fraud would likely emerge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And since all financial institutions would be involved by law, the market would deepen rapidly keeping such insurance costs sufficiently low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such developments could well be the unintended but welcome side effect of making our system recognise a truly equitable distribution of losses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government seems to be aware of the potential benefits of insurance mechanisms of this nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate that pricing could ultimately be prohibitive, one is left to wonder why the notion of insurance does not, at the very least, warrant a deeper and further study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, even the limited liability insurance scheme – one that caps the maximum amount of fraud-related payout – would still be preferable to a system that is entirely bereft of such protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will close with a discussion on why demand side measures, while useful at the margin, are ultimately inadequate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Banks have already independently implemented certain features to introduce additional frictions into online transactions in collaboration with MAS and the Association of Banks Singapore (ABS).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One is to implement a cooling-off period after a charge is made to the maximum daily transfer limit or other key account features.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another step banks can consider: introduce their own hurdles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, one could require certain classes of account holders, such as the elderly or less tech-savvy to opt into a scheme where they designate a separate individual, such as a trusted associate or a family member as a second key who will need to provide approval for transactions that are anomalous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this will almost certainly bring problems of conflict and control of their own, such as when even well-meaning family members impose restrictions on others' use of their own funds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are many instances of careful instructions by scammers building on the trust, naivety or simply insecurity of the victims that lead them to consciously circumvent such circuit breakers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But for the reasons I have offered, I do not believe that it fulfils its fundamental promise of being fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has led to a steady erosion of trust in digital transactions, one that if not addressed expeditiously, could result in the crisis of confidence over online payments and digital finance.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: About five years ago, SG Nasi Lemak Telegram group was first created.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: About half a year ago, a dating show created by a TitTok content creator garnered criticism for its lack of sensitivity in the way it featured and seemed to exploit individuals with special needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For one of my resident's grandmother, it was lost over 115 transactions and six days.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was the result of an online scam.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the last week, articles report that the UK police are investigating a reported case of alleged gang rape of a teenager's virtual avatar in the metaverse.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many, the digital world offers validation, connection and convenience.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, it can also lead to cyber abuse, trolling and painful scams that is often debilitating, in particular, for vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Society is changing more rapidly than ever, with new technologies affecting every aspect of life, from emails after work hours to WhatsApp group chats for classes and sharing locations at the tap of the screen.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: COVID-19 also pushed much of our world online, from grocery shopping to Zoom meetings.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But access to these technologies and competence to use them is not enough to deal with the dangers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to go beyond this, towards digital well-being and digital citizenship for every individual to feel included and empowered to safely participate in the online sphere.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has been taking great steps to this end, in particular, towards digital access and taking a stand against technology-facilitated sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, MCI's Digital for Life Fund funds inclusion projects that empower all Singaporeans to embrace digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it will take the whole-of-society to create a safer online space; and today I will speak on content, communication and cyber habits, three Cs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every day, an approximate 34 million videos are posted to TikTok and 15 million Telegrams are sent, the digital kind.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our modern society craves content and loves to create it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, algorithms open up opportunities for creators to reach large audiences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the curation of perfect content may be harmful to self-esteem.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Studies have shown that social media use appear to play a role in perpetuating negative body concepts and exacerbate eating disorders.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Young girls and boys are pushed videos and tips on unrealistic body expectations and radical diets.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This idea of a filtered life also creates discontent and intensifies social comparisons.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Pressure to create videos which draw quick likes also can lead to unverified or sensationalised content where truth is sacrificed for popularity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, some users, including impressionable miners create suggestive content for validation, at times egged on by peers or malicious actors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is different from adult content creators who are in control of their actions and aware of consequences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I call on platforms and apps to step up age-assurance measures to better protect young users from harmful content and have not placed better verification and restriction measures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, it is not enough in an empowered digital society to simply elect to ban our youths from using their devices or confiscate them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must also create a safe environment for them to turn to during their curiosity and to receive trusted and effective support in unfortunate circumstances.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, I have spoken about the number of social media channels selling, encouraging and circulating non-consensual and illegally obtained sexually explicit materials.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What steps can we take to prevent such heinous acts by perpetrators and protect women and girls who are also our mothers or sisters and our friends?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we hold online forums and social media services accountable?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The longer they permit such harmful content to circulate and improve timeliness in responding to user reports where servers are located overseas, how can we prevent such incidents from happening again?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most importantly, good online habits start from a compassionate and safe offline world built on respect.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Incidents of sexual online harms often involve elements of power and humiliation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to gain control over their victims, perpetrators of sexual violence tend to resort to practices, such as manipulation and coercion.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Offenders may not necessarily find the act gratifying in itself, but in the meaning attributed to power for men and this may override the goals of such acts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end the kind of content we create to regulate and amplify about women is key.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we promote gender equity messages based on merit and move beyond stereotyping objectification and hyper-sexualisation?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond content, the online space is also a place for us to converse with each other.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But in a world of strangers who comment more than communicate and hold different and divergent views, how do we create a respectful space?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Often times, regretfully, we see comments expressing racist or rude remarks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At times, these are disguised as fairy comments or posted by unnamed troll accounts whose creators would perhaps not make such comments to a person's face in real life, but feel empowered hiding behind the veil online.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While their grievances may be authentic, we must do better in digital education such that our people do not lose basic compassion or tolerance for each other and understand the consequences of their words posted in a rage.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we reach beyond algorithms and filter bubbles which seem to confirm our existing beliefs and biases without exception, while hiding content that challenges our thinking?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such bubbles lead to a polarised and fragmented society where even real-life friends are unable to engage with ideas or opposing frequencies that are different from their own.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On cyber habits and how we integrate social media in our day-to-day lives, there are two ends of the spectrum.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the fear of technology which prevents participation such as seniors would deliberately avoid stalls that exclusively use e-payments; and on the other hand, individuals who may get addicted to social media and excessively consume content or participate in online gambling.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we better equip individuals of all ages and literacy levels with positive cyber habits?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Community-based digital interventions and innovations are key ways through which we as a people can take ownership and do something about these issues.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, NUGU, a group-based application has been used to improve self-regulated smartphone usage and has been proven effective.
