speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my constituency, Cheng San-Seletar, a group of youths known as the Cheng San Chapalang Club held one-on-one digital workshops in various languages and dialects for seniors to boost their literacy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Non-profits, such as Cyber Youth Singapore, play an important part too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond programmes, ultimately, it comes down to the fostering of a positive and trusting Internet culture.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is particularly important towards ensuring that every individual can participate fully, including our friends with special needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Studies have shown that the online life may provide a sense of safety, for example, for individuals who autism.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the digital space, they have increased control over their communication and engagement styles, fostering a greater sense of tranquility during these interactions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What more can the Government do to equip and empower persons with special needs towards digital participation and independent living?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Technology can be a great leveller, where you find support in online communities who have the same rare disease as you or date online or visit places in virtual reality that you may never get the chance to see in real life or be the hero in a team game.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But this can only happen if persons with special needs can tap on assistive technology and learn digital skills in a way that is tailored to their understanding of the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there plans to further scaffold our digital structure, for example, by creating specialised websites to cultivate accessible and inclusive online platforms?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, societal efforts must be bolstered by rigorous policies and law enforcement.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the velocity of technological advancement increases, it can be hard for regulators to keep pace and in the grey zone, at times, the de facto rules are set by dominant actors who may not have the public's interest at heart.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From data privacy, content regulation, online harms and AI, jurisdictions from the European Union (EU) to the US to Australia have also been developing new regulations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The digital space does not always stop at physical borders and the fragmentation of digital governance and regulations may see a confusing patchwork of laws where malicious individuals exploit and play in the gaps, for examples, scammers who hide behind confusing IP addresses.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the end of the day, it is the innocent victims who suffer.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond effective investigation, how can we better provide emotional and mental support to victims of online scams who may feel a deep sense of loss and injustice?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Enforcement is also key and social media platforms play a major role.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By having the community play a bigger role in reviewing content and building trust and safety, this leads to a more resilient Internet culture.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Technology helps us but it can also hurt us.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that our digital community builds trust in each other, regardless of age and background, by: Understanding how the algorithm works and exercising care to avoid becoming so immersed in the algorithm until we no longer consider other views.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may also become entangled in narrow-minded views because of what is being shown to us, and such content can potentially create tension in society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, it is important for us to cultivate healthy online habits, so that we can benefit from the use of technology in our day-to-day lives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, communicate judiciously, even when we are behind a screen.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While technology has given many people a chance to speak out about issues that they believe in, it has also become a platform for online harms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The ability to conceal identities behind a screen has given confidence to many "keyboard warriors", thus emboldening them to make comments online in a way that they do not dare to say or do to someone directly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The question is not how we stem the tide but how we can rapidly change the way we respect and protect one another as a digital community, as equal participants of an online world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Tin, in her speech, suggested several strategies and emphasised the need to adopt a comprehensive whole-of-nation approach, working together with private and public sectors in developing an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My speech comes from an educational perspective and focuses on shared responsibility, awareness and accountability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In 2014, Singapore embarked on the Smart Nation initiative, with the vision to develop a "Singapore where people will be more empowered to live meaningful and fulfilled lives, enabled seamlessly by technology, offering exciting opportunities for all".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, we have progressed well, with notable transformation in key domains such as health, transport, finance and education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: According to the 2023 Smart City Index published by Swiss Business School, Institute for Management Development, Singapore is the smartest Asian city and the seventh in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We must, however, do more to guarantee that everyone, regardless of age, race or social background, fully benefits from digital services and is able to meaningfully participate in the digital world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before sharing my perspective on what more can be done to build an inclusive and safe digital society, I would like to note some concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Point of concern, more than 50% of the victims of these crimes were young adults aged 20 to 39.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Tactics adopted by the scammers are also changing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Just last week, the media reported a cyber-kidnapping scam that took place in the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In that case, the victim was a 17-year-old foreign student.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The digital space is not immune to the social issues that exist in the physical world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Online harassment, discrimination and hate speech are widespread, affecting individuals of all ages and from diverse backgrounds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This was highlighted by the hon Member Ms Jessica Tan and Ms Nadia Samdin.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The data also shows that we are aware of the extent of the problem and that we have been progressively trying to mitigate the situation with robust legislation and regulations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to commend the Government for being proactive and for constantly keeping track of these issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to thank the many community agencies who continue to support victims of crime and provide preventive education programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Their involvement reinforces the need to work collaboratively and in partnership with the community sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we adopt a whole-of-nation approach, it is crucial to recognise the role played by community agencies in working with victims and potential perpetrators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Now that I have highlighted some of the current challenges, I would like to share my thoughts on potential strategies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, to unlock these potentials requires trust and shared responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike most other nations where technological innovation is driven by the private sector, in Singapore, the Government has taken a central role in this space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This approach has yielded notable results, placing Singapore at the forefront of global advancements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For example, with over half a million Police surveillance cameras and web-based Police portals, Singapore is regarded as one of the world's safest countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we know, safety is fundamental in Maslow's hierarchy of needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Here, in Singapore, we have met this need very well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue to embrace digitalisation, we have also been working towards the active engagement of citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, we also need to work towards cultivating a shared sense of responsibility and nurture active citizenry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As the Head of Public Safety and Security programme at Singapore University of Social Sciences, I have been working with several groups of students to address issues of cyber crime, scams and specifically, technology-facilitated sexual violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am proud to share that since 2020, students from my programme have, with support from community agencies, developed several community engagement projects to raise awareness on technology-facilitated sexual violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: One of the key learning points from this project is the need to engage young people to be proactive and to tap on their connections to raise awareness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is critical to foster a culture of inclusivity by involving those who are likely to use digital services and be harmed by such services, as well as suggesting and implementing effective mechanisms to prevent unlawful behaviours, young people are also able to assist to address the root causes of such behaviours by educating those who may become perpetrators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Such initiatives also provide opportunities to engage young people who may experience mental health issues to come forward and seek assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, while the Government and the private sector, including companies, have a role to play, cybersecurity attacks are often directed at consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Empowering individuals with the knowledge and skills to navigate the digital world is fundamental.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we progress with our Smart Nation initiative, with a focus on innovation and increasing productivity, we should simultaneously strengthen digital literacy for all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we can ensure that everyone, regardless of age or background, can harness the benefits of technology while understanding the associated risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is equally important to recognise that empowerment is not just about having the power to do certain things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is also about developing responsible behaviours and accountability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is more than just sharing and informing individuals the "dos and don'ts".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: More needs to be done to truly empower individuals to act and be responsible in safeguarding their privacy and the privacy of others in the digital world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Positive reinforcement can motivate citizens to actively contribute to the well-being of their communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Parents play an important role in shaping a generation that acts wisely and responsibly in the digital world by providing good guidance and support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Values that need to be taught to children within this context include awareness of the law, safeguarding privacy, managing reputation, as well as considering the impact of their online behaviour on themselves and the global digital community. : During the COVID-19 pandemic, the use of digital tools became a necessity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Digital tools allowed the world to continue moving, to remain economically viable by allowing work to be done remotely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Adults were not the only recipient of this advancement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Children and young people relied on digital tools extensively for education and for play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We were in a crisis mode then, and we had to react and improvise quickly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Now that we are in a stable environment, it is important that parents and teachers support and guide children on how to communicate and collaborate safely and responsibly in online environments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Just as all children need help from their parents and teachers to become good citizens, today's young people, known as digital natives, also need guidance to learn how to apply citizenship principles in the digital world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Together, let us shape a Singapore, a Smart Nation that is also a safe nation, with digital society embodying the finest qualities of humanity – a society that is resilient, inclusive and founded on the principles of equality and respect.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And as what Assoc Prof Razwana has just shared with us earlier, it is with mutual trust and shared responsibility, with corporations and community partners continuing to equip users with the right skillsets to function in this rapidly-transforming digital society or providing accessibility options for those who are unable to do so, while helping to deter online threats, such as scams, and educating the public about them at the same time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am pleased to note that in the recent years, several of our Woodgrove community partners are already making efforts to make this digital society more accessible for all in our community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One good example can be found in the POSB Woodlands West branch, situated in Woodgrove's Fuchun Neighbourhood Centre.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After its renovation, the branch now exclusively offers self-service banking options that are available 24/7, with branch staff continuing to be present during the bank's usual operating hours to guide customers, especially our seniors, on how to access their desired services with the new teller machines.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The branch also features a community space specially for conducting talks and seminars in various languages that aim to educate residents further regarding digital banking and e-payment services.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I must also register my appreciation for the Singapore Digital Office (SDO)'s Digital Ambassadors who, in 2023, have supported a total of 12 senior-centric community events in Woodgrove, such as our Seniors' Carnival and digital upskilling workshops.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding that the SG Digital Community Hub at our Fuchun Community Centre had to be closed due to the Community Centre's ongoing major upgrading works, the SDOs continue to work closely with our grassroots organisation to operate roving counters at various Woodgrove locations to raise awareness and motivate our residents to adopt digital technologies and enhance their digital skills.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite these efforts, however, many of our seniors in Woodgrove have shared with me that, notwithstanding that they are now equipped with smart phones, they are still apprehensive about exploring and navigating the digital world on their own, even though they are now well capable of using mobile apps like Facebook and WhatsApp to stay in touch with their family and friends.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This does not come as a surprise to me, as they are constantly made aware of heart-wrenching stories from fellow Singaporeans who have suffered great financial loss after falling prey to online scams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The amount was meant to enable the couple to go on their Haj pilgrimage and to see them through their remaining years after retirement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With news and anecdotes of scams like these being reported on an almost daily basis, how do we ensure that Singaporeans, especially our seniors, attain sufficient trust in the safety of the various digital platforms to begin to use them confidently, yet remain vigilant against the ever-evolving risks?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that large organisations, such as banks and e-commerce platforms, will need to do more to prevent losses from online scams and bear their consequences.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just like what Dr Tan Wu Meng had shared earlier, the approach ought to be consumer protection-centric.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just two days ago, I attended to one of my Woodgrove residents, Mr Yu, during our weekly Meet-the-People Session, where he shared about his unpleasant experience with his bank since June last year.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But despite his request to terminate them immediately, Mr Yu was advised by the bank's customer service officer that because the monies have yet to be received by the scammer, he would have to wait until he received his next monthly statement of account as proof before raising a dispute on the fraudulent credit card transactions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To add insult to injury, the bank in their written response reminded him "to always take care of your credentials and refer to the bank's website for more information about how to protect from scams." It is, therefore, understandable that Mr Yu remains aggrieved and perplexed as to why the bank had refused his request to terminate these fraudulent transactions in time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What else could he have done or done better?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What should others who find themselves in similar situations do?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By taking such an approach, it could deter more from becoming active participants in our digital society and cause more to lose faith in our banks' credibility.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is the joint responsibility of all stakeholders to commit towards adopting a whole-of-nation approach to sustain trust by building an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, the banks could and should do more to contribute, such as adopting better anti-phishing solutions, improving authenticity verifications, and being extra vigilant towards abnormal transactions to keep accounts secure and prevent the likelihood of scams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The children of the elderly couple I spoke about earlier who had lost their entire life savings due to an impersonation scam, have shared with me that banks could have done more to prevent these unauthorised transactions from taking place.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amongst other efforts, the banks ought to have paid more attention to each customer's regular banking patterns.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In their parents' case, the couple's bank account had zero withdrawal activity for years until the scammers wiped out over half a million dollars of their savings through two large transactions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The bank should have made calls to them to seek confirmation on the abnormal request before releasing the funds.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are other solutions that may help in terms of safeguarding funds against scams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Concurrently, we should also step-up collaborations between financial institutions and our community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Upskilling workshops, such as OCBC's Digital Silvers programme, and the digital literacy partnership by DBS Foundation and IMDA, are prime examples of such initiatives.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If deployed in conjunction with the previously mentioned measures, the banks can also make use of these workshop as opportunities to promote and encourage seniors to sign up for the "money-lock" features as well as enrolling for the anti-scam insurance to protect funds in their bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that such workshops can be made easily available, just like those run by the SDOs, and I will explore how I can best help my Woodgrove residents benefit from them.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   In recent years, scams continue to evolve, especially online scams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The ever-changing scam methods have made many Singaporeans, especially the seniors, feel very anxious and helpless.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore is not the only country targeted by the scammers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As technologies progress, countries all around the world are facing the thorny issue of how to fight scams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Australia, in 2022, the loss amounted to about S$2.6 billion.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Neighbouring countries, like Malaysia, reported in December last year that between January to November, the amount of loss amounted to as high as RM1.3 billion.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we prevent ourselves from becoming the next target of these scammers?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some seniors have adopted the "see no evil, hear no evil" approach to stay safe by not trying at all.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my opinion, that is certainly not ideal and will cause them to fall behind even more in keeping up with the fast-paced transforming digital society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, in countries like China, online purchase and mobile payments have become an integral part of Chinese society, with cash payment becoming quickly a thing of the past.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Meanwhile, corporations such as banks should also work in tandem to enhance digital safety nets.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Together, we can work our way towards boosting public confidence, and nurture an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) agrees that a whole-of-nation approach to build an inclusive and safe digital society is very much needed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As society digitalised over the past decade, there has been an increase in the prevalence of many varieties of online scams which has lowered the trust level of many Singaporeans in digital tools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Horror stories abound of people losing their life savings in a twinkling of the eye.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, my parents gave me half their life savings to put in my bank account, not in theirs, because they are not confident of not losing it to scams.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their trust level in the security of their money in their bank account has never been so low in their entire lives.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure that many other Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Singaporeans share my parents' sentiment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, the Government has been promoting financial self-reliance by Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For most of us, our own savings is what we have to rely on to meet our expenses and to live in dignity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any compromise to the security of our savings is a big deal to us.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the gravity of the issue, I feel that the Government can do more to safeguard citizens' savings and foster a strong culture of consumer protection.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two main issues with the SRF.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It only covers phishing scams and does not cover the whole range of other scams including malware scams, Police official scams, investment and love scams.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in the recent case of a family losing their life savings due to downloading malware when they tried to buy organic eggs, the SRF does not help them at all.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, under the SRF, financial institutions are directed to perform four duties: One, impose at least a 12-hour cooling period after activation of digital token during which high-risk activities cannot be carried out.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, send notification alerts for activation of digital token and conduct of high-risk activities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, provide outgoing transaction notifications by way of SMS, email or in-app notification selected by the consumer.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four, provide a 24/7 reporting channel and a self-service feature for consumers to promptly block online payment transfers from their accounts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These four duties do not create a sufficient incentive for financial institutions to proactively protect their customers and to remove potential for fraud from their systems.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While vigilance and personal responsibility of the consumer are a critical line of defence against scams, the average consumer has less resources to protect themselves against scams as compared to financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Financial institutions have the capacity to do more to protect consumers against scams with systems to monitor transactions and detect suspicious payment flows.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Large overseas transactions by individuals who rarely or never perform them should immediately trigger alarm bells within the systems of financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would not affect businesses that regularly perform such transactions and would not be difficult to implement given the scale and capacity of the IT infrastructure at financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In assessing the issue of online scams, there is a trade-off between financial security on the one hand and convenience and productivity on the other.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If banks are totally not liable for any losses, then they have only financial incentives to move more and more towards digital financial transactions and services due to the savings in manpower costs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cost of digital financial transactions come in the form of greater ease of losing huge amounts of money, and it is being borne by bank customers, especially the most vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, banks are in control of the security features in their banking apps and the payment processes, but customers, who have no control over those, pay the price for any inadequacies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is clearly not balanced and hence not tenable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In considering the trade-off between financial security and convenience and productivity, it may be difficult for the authorities to draw a line for everyone.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, when OCBC introduced security features in their banking app that prohibited the downloading of suspicious apps, there were complaints from some customers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is foreseeable that different customers will have different needs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there is no need for a one-size-fits-all.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government to consider a multiple-tiered system with different levels of security versus convenience.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another with lower security features and comes with a 50% reimbursement for customers who need greater convenience.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Banks can adjust the security features in their apps and processes to commensurate with the different level of liabilities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, banks might want to re-evaluate the benefits of requiring a separate physical token.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim had spoken previously about the difficulties of getting one from the bank.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whilst the token is an additional cost for banks, it provides the added security of requiring a second device for the authorisation of transactions, not just a handphone which can be hijacked by malware.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Using again the example of the family involved in the recent egg scam, if a physical token had been required, the family might not have lost their life savings.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are expected to conduct cost benefit analysis in evaluating any investments in additional security measures.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the Government can alter their cost benefit analysis by imposing a loss-sharing arrangement, which can lead to a different decision.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under such a model, both the banks and their customers share the liabilities of any losses due to scams and they both have incentives to be vigilant.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Customers can choose the level of security they are comfortable with.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Banks will have incentives to push online transactions in line with their ability to provide security, thereby ensuring that the development of digital financial transactions is a more balanced and holistic one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The maximum limit on reimbursement helps to limit the banks' exposure and at the same time, ensure that the most protection is given to the most vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another institution to which duties should be assigned to mitigate scams is the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board, where many Singaporeans' life savings are held.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is very worrying that recently, there has been a trend where CPF accounts were emptied by scammers who had taken control of the user's Singpass and bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was only in June 2023 that the CPF Board and GovTech introduced Singpass Face Verification as a step-up authentication challenge for certain CPF e-services.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This includes those CPF members who have activated the CPF Withdrawal Lock, which instantly sets the daily withdrawal limit to $0.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singpass Face Verification is required for changing the withdrawal limit.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it strengthen the protection to require CPF members who have activated the CPF Withdrawal Lock to change the withdrawal limits in person at a CPF service centre, similar to the arrangements for the banks' money lock accounts?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same duties that we impose on banks to protect the savings of bank customers should also similarly be imposed on the CPF Board to protect the retirement savings of CPF members.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have seen examples of how scammers can take control of victims' Singpass.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned about the wealth of information available in Singpass.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Information like family members, education background, income and CPF information and so on.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If scammers took control of victims' Singpass, would they not gain very comprehensive information about individual victims and their family members, to enable them to device more ways of scamming?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this wide range of information necessary and would the Government consider re-introducing physical tokens for Singpass?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the Progress Singapore Party supports today's Motion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is crucial for our country to establish an inclusive and secure digital society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, there has been a surge in fraud cases, causing much concern among many citizens.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, my parents split half of their savings into my bank account for safekeeping, fearing that they might fall victim to fraud and lose their hard-earned money.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe many elderly citizens share the same sentiment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, the Government has advocated self-reliance amongst citizens.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, for many citizens, their savings are the only means to ensure they can live with dignity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Online fraud has seriously affected citizens' confidence in the safety of their savings.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can do more to safeguard citizens' savings and protect consumers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the Shared Responsibility Framework released by the MAS and IMDA, there is still insufficient incentive for financial institutions to proactively protect consumers and eliminate potential fraud within their systems.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party urges the Government to consider implementing a multitiered Shared Responsibility Framework.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this framework, consumers can make trade-offs between security and convenience.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If consumers choose an application with lower security features, the losses borne by the bank will be lower.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will give consumers more choices and, at the same time, incentivise banks to provide more secure online transactions, striking a better balance between digitalisation and security in our country. : Mr Speaker, as a nation, we need to adopt a proactive and holistic approach to fight scams and create an inclusive and safe digital society for all.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This makes Singaporeans the most attractive targets for scammers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is much more we can do as a nation to create a safer digital society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us all work together to achieve this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think almost everyone here shares my experience of hearing gut wrenching stories of residents who have seen their life savings wiped out by online scams.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my early days as an MP, an appeal by a group of girls whose faces had been superimposed on sexually explicit photos spreading on social media not only in Singapore but in neighbouring countries shook me to the core.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will forever be grateful to Minister Shanmugam and Minister of State Rahayu for their assistance in expediting justice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I support much o f what colleagues before me have said on the need to sustain trust and build an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I join this debate because I believe the implications of AI and, in particular, the lightning fast development of generative AI (GenAI) on an inclusive and safe digital society deserves special consideration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I said then, "The progress in AI is both exciting and worrying at the same time... we need our AI strategies, policies and people to keep pace with the breathless development.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, let us buckle up." In relation to the online space, the rapid development of AI and GenAI poses many risks: misinformation and disinformation, lack of transparency, privacy concerns, ethical concerns, data leaks, bias, economic inequalities, copyright violations, security risk, concentration of power and more.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The accessibility of GenAI allows anyone on the Internet to manipulate the tool itself as well as the content it can produce, with potentially devastating consequences.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, while chatbots like ChatGPT are now specifically trained to reject harmful prompts like "how to build a dirty bomb", they can still be fooled by bad actors pretending to be doing a research paper or writing a movie script.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Nowadays, we are urged to be careful and skeptical of what we take in and do online, to question everything we see online.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some have asked, are we now to be distrustful by default?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is a very serious question, one that I hope all of us in Parliament will reflect upon.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Think back to the Ah Ma who did not open the Healthier SG enrolment SMS from MOH.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In the business world, there are companies that have blocked GenAI tools from their systems.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What happens when "distrustful by default" turns into "distrust and drop-out"?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is what gives us the confidence to interact and transact online.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is needed to drive innovation and adoption in order to reap the considerable benefits of digital and AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we want AI to uplift Singapore's economic and social potential, if we want Singapore and Singaporeans to be at the vanguard in developing, deploying, adopting and innovating technology, we need our people to be satisfied that the products and services they consume are safe.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we are going to ride in a racecar, we have got to trust the brakes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Most, if not all major platforms, have put in some form of brakes or safeguards.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Safeguards can take the form of policies, practices and tools, such as robust community guidelines, content moderation policies and ensuring that data is representative and scrubbed for bias.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Machine learning and AI itself will play a powerful role in creating new types of safeguards and building trust.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Machine learning tools can be used to ensure privacy and trust by design and to detect and block fraudulent transactions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They can also be tuned to make the right tradeoffs in proportion to the risks involved.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI tools can also reduce bias – both human bias as well as bias that has crept into machine learning models.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By enabling the identification and measurement of bias, they allow platforms to take steps to reduce discrimination and bias or to de-bias the algorithms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A well-known example is Airbnb, which has used data and machine learning to reduce discrimination, for example, against black guests and black hosts and promote inclusion on its platform.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My position has not changed from when I made my speech in April.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The response to the associated risks cannot be fear and paralysis, but rather to equip ourselves with the knowledge, strategies and tools to navigate these risks, including to use AI itself to keep propelling us forward.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To that end, I offer give suggestions, building on some of the suggestions of my colleagues, to sustain trust by building an inclusive and safe digital society in the age of AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While it will never feel timely enough for those who suffer from the harm, the Government is proactively taking steps to safeguard safety and inclusion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The approach taken by the Government has been one of engagement and utilising a range of levers, not just legislation but also voluntary adoption of codes of practice and tools, to ensure effectiveness – and I would add sustainability – before making them mandatory.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is an approach that engenders trust and buy in, helping to take away some of the usual impediments to move.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, Singapore was one of the world's first to introduce regulations to ensure designated social media services take preventive measures to ensure online safety.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, the UK Online Safety Act was delayed some five to six years, falling victim to political crises making it very hard to move.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some of the measures to combat scam such as the mandatory registration of all alphanumberic SMS sender IDs with the Singapore SMS Sender ID Registry (SSIR) would be hard to pull off in many other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The hon Member Sylvia Lim has said that we are moving towards a crisis of confidence in digital transactions and banking, without stronger intervention by Government regulators.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe the Government has taken important steps, but I also believe they will continue to take more.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Minister will provide an update on the implementation of recently announced measures and share additional measures the Government may be exploring, including expanding potentially the scope of some of the restrictions on other platforms such as online technology platforms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has taken a pragmatic approach to AI regulation – we should not rush to regulate what we do not yet understand, when the solutions are not yet clear – is how I would articulate it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Rather, the approach has been, again, one of engagement, of testing different solutions and of building capacities while recognising that legislation will come at some point.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding, the Government should continue to review the adequacy of safeguards and provisions in the Online Safety Act to protect against AI-generated content.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At this point, I would like to ask the Minister if she is looking to introduce any AI focused protective measures in the near future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In particular, I echo the concerns said by many on deepfakes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The US Executive Order seeks to establish standards and best practices for detecting AI-generated content and authenticating official content, with the Department of Commerce tasked to develop guidance for content authentication and watermarking.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There seems to be momentum behind reviewing the safeguards against harmful deepfakes and parsing out accountability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is also the risk, as highlighted by the hon Member Tan Wu Meng, on democracy itself.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, there are calls to require that in any interaction with AI, be it text, image or voice, the AI has to declare that it is AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In addition, we have to think of how to support individual victims whose images may have been exploited in deepfakes and harmed – a highly traumatic experience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, engage in a whole-of-nation partnership between all stakeholders in the online ecosystem to educate and empower our people, especially the young and the old, on scams, online harms and digital literacy, including AI literacy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While the tech platforms can and must do more, an inclusive and safe digital society requires the concerted effort of many more stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These stakeholders include the Government, the public sector, the private sector, the tech platforms, but also telcos, banks, AI companies and other companies offering products and services online, law enforcement agencies, parents and caregivers, schools, social services and community organisations, and at the centre of it all, the individuals themselves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI literacy refers to as a set of competencies that enables people to critically evaluate, communicate and collaborate effectively with AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yesterday, Minister Chan Chin Sing shared how the Ministry of Education (MOE) is preparing students in our schools and IHLs by developing their foundational knowledge of AI, promoting safe and responsible use of AI, measures to guard against the risks of AI and teaching cyber wellness skills, such as evaluating information and identifying fake news.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is nascent interest on AI literacy in early childhood education, with some promising effects.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some studies have highlighted how early AI literacy can improve many aspects of child development, such as creative inquiry, emotional inquiry and collaborative inquiry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some argue that with more well-designed AI toys and services such as PopBots, Zhoria, Quickdraw, young children could explore AI-related concepts and develop their digital and AI literacy, even if they may not know and understand the knowledge behind it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Others argue that since young children are already using devices and tablets, it is important that they attain some elements of data literacy even at a young age, such as understanding the concepts of personal data and data privacy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, there are also question marks like whether age-appropriate curriculums can be developed for early childhood, the readiness of early childhood educators themselves and concerns over inequalities and inclusiveness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Does the Minister see AI literacy in early childhood as a worthwhile investigation?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The focus will be on directing AI towards addressing big challenges, not just locally, but globally like climate change and population health, as well on empowering individuals, business and community to use AI with confidence, discernment and trust.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not only will the AI itself create value, it will build capability within the Government as multi-disciplinary product teams will learn to make adjustments and deploy solutions to address weaknesses that surface and policy teams will learn how to prevent the spread of harmful activities and to shape effective regulations by doing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We start in an enviable position, where there is strong trust in the Government, hard earned over decades.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If the Government is transparent on the value as well as the risks as it deploys these high-value use cases, if we are able to advance research into Online Trust and Safety and build and test tools and solutions, such as "Trust by Design" technologies like watermarking and content authentication and use these tools in these use cases in the public sector, Singapore can set an example for the private sector and governments around the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, take the lead in adopting responsible AI across the digital economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Responsible AI is a holistic approach to developing, assessing and deploying AI systems in a safe, trustworthy and ethical way that spans the full product life cycle.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It entails being transparent about when and how products leverage AI, how algorithms influence decisions and the steps being taken to mitigate bias, privacy violations and other risks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The value of responsible AI goes beyond risk mitigation; it can strengthen trust between organisations and their customers, assuring customers that the products and services they consume are safe.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The public sector and companies across sectors in the digital economy deploying AI solutions, whether in developing their products and services or supply chain AI , should operationalise responsible AI as fast as they build and deploy AI solutions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because Responsible AI demands teams of individuals with different expertise, experiences and background and cooperation across the organisation at all levels, the Prime Minister and chief executive officers themselves leading from the top to drive and sustain investment and focus is required.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And lastly, increase the international cooperation on Online Safety, including AI governance and safety.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Given the global nature of the cyberspace, driving dialogue, sharing knowledge and cooperating on solutions is important.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Boosting inclusive AI governance and interoperability to achieve our shared goal of trustworthy AI is something that Singapore must commit to do and can seek to play a key role in.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The open sourcing of AI Verify, cited by the Member Ms Sylvia Lim earlier, is actually a way of promoting international cooperation and putting a claim on some intellectual leadership and legitimacy in this space.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Non trivial, when parties involve actually do have some tensions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Another global issues like climate change, Singapore has led the way on some fronts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Minister Grace Fu's leadership of negotiations on Article 6 and mitigation at successive COPs come to mind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I know it sometimes feels like you are playing whack a mole.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I hope the nation will rise to this call for each of us to play our part in order to continue closing the trust gap between the online and physical space.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Across our nation, residents, both young and old, tech savvy and not, have fallen victim to these fraudulent schemes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have met constituents who have lost their entire life savings to scammers, with even fixed deposit accounts being cleared out by these criminals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some have joint accounts with their children or parents, doubling the impact on families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These incidents demonstrate a concerning vulnerability that affects us all.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I consider myself relatively tech savvy, I have to admit that even I feel the looming threat of becoming a victim one day.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many victims I have spoken to describe a disheartening response from their banks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Upon reporting the fraud, they frequently receive responses that are frustratingly vague or non-committal.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They offer little information citing banking secrecy, and at times, a goodwill payment that does not fully cover the loss.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Victims are sometimes told by the Police that the funds had been transferred overseas and nothing further can be done to retrieve the funds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The technical nature of these scams is deeply concerning.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Drive-by download attacks and the more advanced zero-day exploits make it possible for malware to be installed on phones with little or no user action.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These methods exploit vulnerabilities in operating systems and applications.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In view of these sophisticated attacks, how far do the authorities investigate each reported scam, especially those involving screen reading and key logging malware?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Without thorough investigations, it will not be possible to ascertain fault and ensure that innocent victims are not held responsible for losses that they did not cause.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is the default blame then placed on the victims, who have to bear most of the financial loss?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Scams have emerged as a formidable obstacle to advancing digital access for our citizens, particularly in our senior community.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Numerous elderly residents I have encountered expressed a fear of using internet banking or online payments because they are apprehensive about falling prey to scams.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Consequently, I find myself hesitant to advocate the use of digital banking to them, despite its convenience, due to the real risk of them losing their entire life savings if they are targeted by scammers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This situation has precipitated what Member for Aljunied, Ms Sylvia Lim, as she describes, as a crisis with confidence with the digital banking system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unless the authorities address the issues of scams more effectively and establish stronger consumer protections, our extensive efforts to transition all our citizens into a digitally empowered society will come to naught.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One tool the Government has on hand to deal decisively with scams is the Online Criminal Harms Act.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will allow the Government to, inter alia, direct online platforms to disable access to accounts suspected to be involved in scams.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it is only set to be progressively rolled out this year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When will the Online Criminal Harms Act be fully operationalised?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Multi-factor authentication relies on a combination of something you know and something you have.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, when phones are compromised by malware, allowing scammers to view screens and keystrokes, this system collapses into a single factor.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This allows scammers who have access to the password entered by the user to bypass the additional security layer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, bringing back physical tokens will reinstate the crucial second layer of security.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MAS must more assertively and decisively tackle the problem of scams in the banking system to protect consumers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my dealings with MAS, when advocating for constituents victimised by scams, I have observed that MAS tends to forward these critical cases to the banks for their follow-up instead of directly addressing and resolving the issues on behalf of victims.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This delegation process then places the onus on the banks to determine who is at fault, the institution or the victim, for the occurrence of the scam.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such a practice raises serious concerns about the impartiality and effectiveness on the investigation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have also observed a discrepancy in MAS' approach to enforcing actions on financial institutions for different violations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MAS should require banks to tackle scams with the same level of intensity and rigour as they do in safeguarding consumers interest for system outages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Scam victims need a comprehensive explanation from a knowledgeable and impartial entity like MAS about how the scam occurred.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This explanation should detail the roles of banks, telcos, customers and other entities in both the occurrence and prevention of such scams.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will determine who is responsible and who should bear the loss, the cost of these fraudulent acts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, responsibility should not be limited to financial institutions, telcos and consumers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Social media companies and mobile phone handset manufacturers should be held accountable for securing their platforms again scams.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Social media platforms should be required to have processes in place to remove fraudulent posts soon after being notified.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of these may be less tech savvy users.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is not reasonable to expect that everyone will have the technical proficiency to keep their devices updated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, consumer protection strategies must be designed on the premise that a significant number of users will not know how to keep their devices updated and should incorporate additional layers of security to safeguard these users.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A central agency should oversee all scam investigations and responses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am aware of the Anti-Scam Command (ASCom) and the important work their officers are doing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, given that ASCom is a department under the Commercial Affairs Department of the Singapore Police Force, I do not think it can be held accountable for whole-of-Government efforts to combat scams.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Who therefore, is ultimately accountable for the Government's anti-scam efforts?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, MAS should take a more active role in acertaining responsibility for scams carried out on banks, digital platforms and supporting victims.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, the Online Criminal Harms Act needs to be fully operational operationalised without further delay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our actions in the face of this scourge will determine our commitment to protecting our citizens in the digital age.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us act swiftly and decisively to protect our people and indeed, ourselves.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, the narrative was interrupted by the rise of the socially conscious investor.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The socially conscious investor demanded that corporations be held accountable to higher standards of social responsibility.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This has in turn, led to the emergence of corporate social responsibility and ESG, or environmental, social and governance goals as new priorities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In response to the Motion, I would like to update Friedman’s question to today’s context: In a digital-driven economy and society, what is a socially responsible business and its role in society?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As a Labour advocate, I would like to highlight three trends that are worrying and offer three suggestions of how we could respond as a society.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, technologies will get more complicated and powerful.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us appreciate the convenience that technologies such as booking or buying apps bring to us.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In exchange for the convenience, we might consent to our data being re-marketed by these companies behind these apps.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Given the fluid nature of data, users might find themselves at the receiving end of unsolicited marketing messages as companies seek to profit from new consumer segments.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many individuals struggle to extricate themselves from the never-ending web of marketing messages as they lack the knowledge or ability to do so.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The struggle imposes mental strain on individuals who are constantly inundated by advertisements and often tempted to spend more time and more money on the apps.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How might we cultivate a respectful code of ethics for commerce in the digital age?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, technologies will get simpler yet more complex.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: On the one hand, mobile technology coupled with AI tools are set to herald a new age of productivity for service frontliners; we do see resources being customised and at the fingertips of service frontliners when interacting with customers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, workers can also be held hostage by technology.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many workers are users and operators, and unexposed or underexposed to technology's working mechanics.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: If companies train workers only for deployment rather than staff development, a firm’s decision to change technology provider could render its current cohort of workers struggling to become competent in a new technology within a short timeframe.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This story would end with the workers being made redundant and the firm let off the hook when the firm cites incompatibility of worker skills and business needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How might we reduce worker precariousness arising from information asymmetry and in its place, cultivate a sense of shared responsibility between companies and workers to enhance workers’ career longevity in a digital economy?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, the spotlight on technology and online harm has made us more aware of our rights.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: However, many of us are less certain of how to exercise them.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: While businesses are conscious of seeking consent from users on data privacy, default privacy settings are often onerous to navigate.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It is even more challenging to attempt a complete opt out from the default settings.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, users who consent to the default settings might not be aware of what the settings allow or mean.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, it would not be far off to consider that the default mindset of these companies to be, and I quote journalist Zeynep Tufekci: "to expect users to accept what they are given, not know their options or not have the constant vigilance required to keep track of the available options, however limited they may be." Workers of technology companies, whether freelancers or employees, are also not spared.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, workers might be required or made to feel obliged to download their employer's or company's app and to always accede to requests to update the apps, unknowing that each update could reset their data privacy settings and void previous opt-outs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As more companies transform into digital for businesses, how might we introduce oversight into the processes by which companies obtain data privacy permissions to ensure accountability and transparency?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Central to the three trends is our expectations of what is a socially responsible business and its role in a digital economy and society.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, a socially responsible company would ensure default settings favour user privacy and autonomy.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This means that users must have unrestricted access to their own data privacy settings.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: There must be avenues for users trapped in unsavoury data privacy settings to get help to set themselves free from the snares of predatory companies.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such help could be in the form of a helpdesk managed by public and private players working together.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, they could work closely with the unions and sector agencies to dial up the digital and technology fluency of their workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This will build up workers' digital capital and is key to workers' career longevity in the digital age.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In an era where digital technology permeates every aspect of our lives, today's Motion holds more relevance than ever.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As an educator and a father to teenagers and young children, I am acutely aware of the impact of a digital world.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It involves safeguarding our young generation's mental health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The digital world has transformed education and communication, offering unparalleled opportunities for learning and connection.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A key player in this transformation is AI.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: AI has revolutionised the educational experience by personalising learning and providing real-time feedback.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In online safety, AI can detect potential dangers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It can identify patterns of cyberbullying, flag inappropriate content and even offer proactive and swift interventions to protect our young users.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When harnessed correctly, AI is a powerful ally.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the deployment of AI has its challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The misuse of perpetuating cyberbullying through deepfakes or other manipulative content is a growing worry.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, if not developed ethically, AI systems can inherit biases, leading to discriminatory practices or inadequate protection for certain groups.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The balance between leveraging AI for safety and respecting individual privacy rights is delicate and requires careful navigation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Another significant challenge in the digital world is the alarming prevalence of cyberbullying.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A global report from 2020 brought to light a "cyber pandemic" affecting children worldwide.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Contributing factors include widespread smartphone ownership, excessive social media use and high gaming activity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The link between social media and mental health issues like anxiety and depression in young users is increasingly evident.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our responsibility is to ensure that digital access does not compromise our children's mental health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Like many of her peers, Aisha was active on various social media platforms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And despite her age, she easily bypassed the age verification processes with a falsified birth date, a common oversight in many platforms' registration procedures.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: On these platforms, Aisha encountered a barrage of challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite these services claiming to have stringent content filters, she was exposed to inappropriate content.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This exposure disturbed her and skewed her understanding of social norms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These were sparked after a harmless AI face swapped picture of her was posted online.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Harassing messages and public ridicule and shaming from anonymous accounts became a daily ordeal, deeply affecting her.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The turning point came when the school intervened, recognising her sudden withdrawal and decline in academic performance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They worked closely with her parents to address the issues she faced online.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But the question is: was it too late?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It became clear that while digital literacy at school and parental involvement at home were crucial, more accountable and stringent policies were needed to complement these efforts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that regard, I would like to highlight a three-pronged approach encompassing schools, homes and the Internet, which we are practising.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continue to instill a culture of ethical and mindful digital engagement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our children must understand the complexities of the online world, discern fact from fiction and build healthy digital relationships.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Topics like online privacy, recognising misinformation and understanding the ethics and psychological impact of digital media are crucial.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continue to creatively integrate these digital literacy programmes into the core curriculum of our education system at all levels.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This integration should not be limited to just IT lessons.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Rather, it should be woven into the fabric of all subjects, where appropriate, to ensure that our children are equipped with digital skills and ethics as a fundamental aspect of their education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The home environment is equally critical in shaping children's digital experiences.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Parents and guardians must be well-informed but most importantly, actively involved.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This can be achieved through regular workshops and resources that empower them to create a safe digital environment at home.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These initiatives should focus on educating parents about online risks, appropriate content monitoring, which many are shy to do and strategies for open communication with their children about their online activities and experiences, a skill not many are willing to do but is crucial in a child's development.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The aim is to foster a collaborative approach between schools and families, ensuring consistency in the messages and practices regarding digital safety and usage.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The gateway to digital experiences must be fortified.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Stringent measures to protect children from online harm, age-appropriate content filters and stricter regulations on digital platforms are necessary to create a safer digital environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I urge social media services and application developers to intensify their age assurance measures.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They must be more vigilant in safeguarding young users from harmful content.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, it is essential that social media services improve their response time to user reports, ensuring that flagged harmful content is acted upon promptly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is worth considering how long these services take to remove harmful content and should we establish a specific timeframe for them to take down such content.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Aisha's story underscores the importance of a robust age verification system, effective content filtering and proactive measures against cyberbullying by these platforms to safeguard our children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As legislators, we must support and enforce such initiatives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must ensure that social media services and application developers comply with these practices and continually evolve their strategies to address emerging online safety challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, we must ensure that this digital world is a safe and inclusive space, especially for our younger generation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In our efforts to build an inclusive and safe digital society, I propose three strategic steps, First, in school, it is important to integrate digital literacy into the curriculum.
