speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is not just about teaching how to use technology, but also about digital ethics, online security and the skills to navigate the digital world responsibly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, at home, where the role of parents is critical.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They need to be equipped with knowledge and resources to create a safe digital environment at home, as well as becoming a partner in their children's digital education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, on the internet, we should fortify the gateway into the digital world.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This means that legislation and policies should be tightened to ensure that Social Media Services and application developers shoulder more responsibility in protecting our children from harmful online content.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through this approach, I hope we can work together as a society to build a digital domain that is not only technologically advanced, but also one that has peace, understanding, and inclusion for all, especially for our younger generation. : Madam, in conclusion, this is a call to action for service providers, lawmakers, educators, parents and the tech industry.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must work together to create policies, educational curricula and technological solutions that safeguard our digital spaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Ensuring the safety of our children in the digital world is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My vision is simple – to see our children safe to explore, to learn and grow without fear and harm.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Motion tabled today has two key thrusts – that our digital society is both inclusive and safe.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: E-commerce, job and phishing scams have quickly become the most prevalent scam types through popular channels like messaging apps, social media and online shopping platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Clearly, as our society becomes more digital, having a safe online environment is of utmost priority.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Numerous phishing websites and mobile applications have emerged recently.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Scammers create fake websites that are almost indistinguishable from the real ones.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Fake websites deceive users into entering their credentials, targeting those who seek to use messaging, email and banking services.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Link shorteners are frequently used by scammers to make these links appear legitimate.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One way to identify fake websites is to carefully examine the domain name.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: An example of a legitimate domain name is ".gov.sg", which cannot be replicated by scammers. "Go.gov.sg" is the official link shortener used by Government agencies and users are prompted to pause and check their browser address bar when they click on the shortened Government link for the first time.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Government also publishes and updates a list of trusted sites and clearly highlights that people should look out for ".gov.sg" in the URL of Government websites.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For a more holistic approach, would it be feasible for the Government to require consumer banking and messaging services to publish such clear advisories and implement measures similar to the "pause and check" feature?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Now, the question arises – in an environment where phishing scams involving clickable links still take place, how do we ensure that all retail banking users, particularly seniors, are aware of this initiative?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, these measures do not apply to non-bank financial institutions, such as digital investment platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Government consider widening the scope of these measures to ensure that non-bank financial institutions serving retail customers also conform to the same standards?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: After all, it is in the interest of end users and service providers when scammers fail in their attempts.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Having considered online safety, I would like to now turn our attention to the other equally important tenet of this Motion.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the rest of my speech I will raise certain issues to ensure that our digital society is also inclusive to disadvantaged groups.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially important as daily life becomes digitalised over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Today, the Internet has become a significant and unparalleled source of data.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: All of us in this Chamber would not think twice to search something up on the web or add to its content through social media.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In day-to-day living, instant payments via our smartphones are second nature.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For some in society, it is not quite the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: According to MCI, seniors in Singapore continue to find using technology for purposes, such as contactless payment, a challenge.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For seniors over the age of 60, this struggle is even more prevalent.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The SG Digital Office (SDO) set up in June 2020 by IMDA runs a Seniors Go Digital programme that aims to help our seniors navigate the digital landscape with ease and confidence.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given that some seniors still express hesitancy over the use of technology, can the Government clarify if such programmes have been successful in achieving their objectives and what more can be done?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on to our friends with sensory disabilities, more attention is required to ensure that they are not left behind as we develop what we call our Digital Social Compact.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I will begin by addressing the concerns of the deaf community, followed by a discussion on issues relating to the visually impaired (VI).

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In September last year, I asked a Parliamentary Question on whether the Government will consider providing Singapore Sign Language (SgSL) interpretation services during significant Government live TV broadcasts.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It was noted in the reply that since April 2020, MCI has required TV broadcasts of significant national and public interest to be accompanied by SgSL interpretation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This move marked a crucial step towards inclusivity and events, such as the National Day Rally and Budget speeches, have, indeed, become more accessible to the deaf community.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, there had been significant live events where SgSL interpretation was absent or only provided in a delayed broadcast.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, during the most recent Presidential Forum in 2023, I understand that SgSL interpretation was not available in realtime but only in a delayed broadcast.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This was despite the fact that the Presidential Election 2023 was the first contested Presidential Elections in over a decade in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Critical live broadcasts, such as the initial COVID-19 briefings during the outbreak of the pandemic, also lacked sign language interpretation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Although it was eventually provided in later briefings, it is essential we recognise the challenging and unsettling environment the deaf community faced during those early, deeply uncertain moments.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond TV broadcasts, there has also been feedback highlighting the disadvantages faced by the deaf community.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Today, in our digital first but not digital only approach, there are still Government services that involve face-to-face or phone interaction.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This includes reporting flat damage to HDB, consulting MOH or health clusters or addressing issues with CPF, ICA, LTA, among others.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These are not fully accessible to the deaf.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The deaf often have no choice but to hire a sign language interpreter at their own expense in order to communicate with Government agencies through these channels.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given these persistent challenges, it is easy to empathise with the deaf community.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is natural for them to feel that their social participation in day-to-day living, access to essential services or time-sensitive information lag behind those of their hearing peers currently.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware and grateful for the ongoing collaboration between ServiceSG and SADeaf in addressing these accessibility challenges.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: That being said, it is necessary that we continue to push for inclusive and timely solutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that no one in the deaf community feels left behind as our world becomes digital.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I will use the final part of my speech to highlight issues on behalf of the visually impaired (VI) community.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These high traffic websites are defined as those with at least one million visits per year.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Enabling Masterplan 2030 rightfully acknowledges the existing gap in digital accessibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It commits to designing accessible websites and applications for Government services.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, it aims to raise the adoption of e-accessibility by the non-Government sectors.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Despite this, on the ground, many of those with VI continue to provide feedback that digital inaccessibility remains a big issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: People with VI consume digital content in a different way.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For those with low to no vision remaining, they use a type of software called a screen reader.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A screen reader is a text-to-speech software that turns a user's phone or computer into a talking machine.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It scans all available text and reads the contents out loud.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For images and buttons, the screen reader needs clear, user-friendly labels or alternate text to enable meaningful audio playback of screen content.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Speaking with the VI community, their experience with accessing digital content in Singapore via their screen readers is riddled with inconsistencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For example, following the latest update of the HealthHub application, I am told that, unfortunately, blind users can no longer access the app like before.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Previously, the app featured well-labelled buttons, enabling blind users to easily book hospital appointments or make bill payments seamlessly.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: After the update, the buttons somehow became unlabelled and the screen reader could only announce "button" or "unlabelled graphic" without any helpful context.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, blind users are left to navigate the app by trial and error, leading to an inefficient and often frustrating experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Visually impaired users have reported positive experiences with other Government websites like IRAS and CPF, showing that with the right focus and consideration, our digital services can, indeed, be made accessible.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from Government services, many websites and applications from local companies are not screen-reader friendly.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For most of us, consuming Government services is not the most significant proportion of our online activity.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This also applies to those who have visual impairments, who engage in diverse online interactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) is an international standard to ensure online content is accessible to persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The WCAG standards have three levels of conformance: "A" being the minimum; "AA" being mid-range; and "AAA" is highest.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There is also no direct incentive for companies to make them accessible for all users or consumers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Without these, companies do not spare enough thought or consideration for disadvantaged groups in their online offerings.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These methods often do not meet the basic level "A" of the WCAG standard, which requires alternative challenge-response authentication to cater to different types of sensory perception.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Examples like this cause persons with disabilities to frequently find themselves relying on others when using the simplest of online services.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They, too, yearn for the autonomy to independently manage their day-to-day activities like you and I.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In our physical built environment, we have the BCA Accessibility Code, which sets minimum accessibility requirements for new developments.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The BCA-administered Accessibility Fund provides capital incentive to improve building accessibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These measures benefit everyone, including the physically disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As goods and services become more digitalised, it becomes equally if not more important to implement similar standards and incentives in the digital domain to ensure accessibility for all.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I fully agree with the hon Member Ms Tin Pei Ling in her opening speech: why should the digital world be different from the real one?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Looking abroad, Singapore can draw inspiration from internationally established frameworks for online accessibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This directive ensures that services are designed for easy use by persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Key measures include providing information in a way that can be perceived by everyone.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This means offering alternatives to supplement non-textual content, using easily readable fonts, ensuring high contrast and allowing adjustable spacing in text.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Shifting our focus from online accessibility frameworks, we must also guarantee that future designers are educated on accessible user experience design and digital inclusion.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To move towards a future where digital accessibility is the norm, it is crucial that these principles are integrated from the very beginning of any new digital venture.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Thoughtful, or should I say, universal design, must be considerate towards those with diverse usage requirements.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Having discussed various challenges and the need for inclusive digital design, I would like to propose three key suggestions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: With the application of these suggestions, we take significant steps towards ensuring that the VI community will, one day, enjoy full inclusion in every aspect of our digital society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government takes the lead, sets the example and facilitates this agenda, we also need corporates, programmers, UX designers and end-users to implement this in practice, safeguard online activity and confidently participate in the digital landscape.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I share the hope of those in the community that with a concerted effort, this digital utopia will not remain a dream, but soon become reality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It fuels our economy, empowers our communities and enriches our lives in countless ways.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But, like any frontier, the digital world also harbors hidden dangers and challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I stand before you today to advocate for a cause close to my heart and one that deserves our urgent attention: ensuring a safe and inclusive digital world for our senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They worked tirelessly, sacrificed immensely and laid the foundation for our nation's success.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Now, as they navigate the twilight of their lives, it is our duty to ensure they can enjoy the fruits of their labor in a world increasingly shaped by technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, for many seniors, the digital revolution presents challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Confusing interfaces, complex online procedures and the ever-present threat of online scams can leave them feeling overwhelmed and excluded.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given the rapid pace of society and the push towards digitalisation, many may have no choice but to go digital to transact, communicate and stay connected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While many seniors possess smartphones, not all know how to use them effectively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may struggle with basic concepts like data versus wi-fi, digital tokens and password management.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I understand this from first-hand experience from helping my parents set up new accounts on their handphones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Downloading the apps and creating the accounts, is but the first step.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The real challenge lies in navigating the maze of features, logins and verifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even with patience and repetition, committing the steps to memory is not easy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The troubleshooting, the fear of getting locked out – they have so many questions and it is not just a one-time fix.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But, what about countless others who face this digital divide without a familiar voice to guide them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I witness these struggles at my Yio Chu Kang Meet-the-People sessions (MPS).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Imagine Mdm Tan, who spent her life nurturing her family, grappling to access online Government services just to pay a bill, due to a lack of accessibility to physical options or clear information about it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Picture Mr Lim, a veteran of our nation's independence who built an honest living from little resources, now feeling a gnawing helplessness as he struggles to decipher a phishing email.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Consider Mr Ahmad and his wife, pillars of our community, building their lives on hard work and friendly smiles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are not hypothetical situations; these are the lived realities of countless seniors in Yio Chu Kang and across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The digital divide is not just a matter of convenience; it is a barrier to essential services, financial independence and social connection.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without proper digital literacy and support, our seniors risk being left behind, isolated and vulnerable to exploitation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Measuring digital literacy for seniors should not be a mere tally of workshops attended or apps downloaded.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Just like learning to cook as a life skill takes more than a single class, using digital tools as a life skill too, requires sustained practice, advancement and exploration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The stakes, however, are higher in the digital realm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A misguided click can vanish years of hard-earned savings, understandably instilling fear and doubt.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This creates a cruel contradiction: urging seniors towards digital dependence on one hand and then, blaming or even mocking them for the costly mistakes made.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Imagine the bewilderment, when the promised convenience suddenly morphs into potential peril.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is no wonder that some seniors, despite making initial progress, choose to retreat entirely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sadly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, the digital world also harbours malicious actors who prey on the seniors' vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From fake investment schemes to impersonation scams, these predators exploit their trust, inflicting financial and emotional harm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The rise of deepfakes further underscores the need to shield our seniors from online predators.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have seen recent troubling instances of deepfakes targeting high-profile figures like our Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister, promoting dubious investment schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These malicious attempts not only sow confusion and erode trust in online information, but also prey on seniors' susceptibility to such scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must not let our seniors become easy targets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must equip them with the knowledge and tools to navigate the digital landscape safely and confidently.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Motion rightly puts that bridging the digital divide and combating online scams require a multi-pronged, whole-of-nation approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must continue to empower seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have started the journey and we must persist.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Building digital literacy for seniors is an ongoing work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need sustainable, engaging programmes woven into the fabric of their lives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Programmes tailored to their needs and interests, where trusted mentors guide them step-by-step, refresh their memories and nurture their confidence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These ongoing journeys will empower seniors to slowly but surely unlock the full potential of technology, one click or one tap at a time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about empowering them to build critical thinking skills and encourage source verification to be more discerning in the online space.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do not just forward messages; check email addresses and never share passwords.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Importantly, our seniors themselves must inculcate a mindset of continuous learning and exercise vigilance about technology and new threats.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must build support systems for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Dedicated helplines and support networks are critical for seniors to seek assistance with digital issues and report scams without fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we consider something like the Municipal Services Office (MSO) or the OneService App?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must strengthen enforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Law enforcement agencies must actively crack down on cyber criminals targeting seniors, bringing them to justice and deterring future scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We know seniors often approach their MPs for help in expediting police investigations to recover lost funds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Her words reflect the emotional toll these situations take, and I quote, "What is the update so far?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I need my money back." Our seniors deserve timely updates and having the confidence that our processes can deliver results.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must improve our infrastructure and cyber resilience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to review the approach to victims of scams by unauthorised transactions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Placing the sole blame on scam victims for such transactions is unfair.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While education is essential, in today's complex digital landscape, losses can stem from vulnerabilities within the system itself.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Larger players, from telcos to banks and app developers, must share responsibility and invest in robust security measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The recent government interventions and efforts are welcome.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, more time and resources are needed to upgrade our infrastructure and ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What about in China, where even elderly citizens are known to navigate online payments with ease?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Learning from best practices abroad can help us build a more secure and inclusive digital ecosystem for all, where convenience does not come at the cost of vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This requires transparency in how we address their concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also demands swift and decisive action to combat these threats, demonstrating that we are truly committed to their well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A timely response to their anxieties and frustrations, like providing updates on investigations to Mdm R, reaffirms their faith in our agencies and processes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By prioritising their safety and empowerment, we can build a digital future where our seniors feel not only included, but also that they are protected and are valued members of the community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the meantime, seniors and vulnerable citizens must not bear the brunt of digital progress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While building cyber resilience takes time, essential services must remain accessible, even if it means facilitating physical options.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot celebrate digital convenience while leaving our elderly behind, inconvenienced and frustrated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Picture Mr Lim laughing alongside his grandchildren in a distant land, brought together by technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Ahmad, enjoying the convenience of purchasing online without fearing that he will lose his life savings from it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not just a vision; it is a promise we can make to our seniors, a promise of a digital world where they are not left behind, but empowered and embraced.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must accelerate digital literacy programmes, equipping every senior with the tools they need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must establish a centralised support network, a single point of contact for their digital anxieties and fears.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must hold accountable, those who target our seniors with swift and decisive action.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let this be our pledge today: we will bridge the digital divide, hand in hand with our Silver Generation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will weave a digital tapestry where their voices are heard, their concerns addressed and their safety enshrined.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not just about technology; it is about respect, inclusion and honouring the legacy they have built.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us, together, build a digital Singapore where every senior, from Mdm Tan to Mr Lim to Mr Ahmad, walks confidently into the future, empowered and as valued members of our community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a point that has been raised by many other hon Members today and I would like to add my views as well, to this discussion.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are large numbers, and by now, I am sure everybody in the House is quite familiar with them.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our approach is for Singapore to be a "Digital First" society, and not a "Digital Only" society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, there is a need to make sure that our non-digital options – where we choose to provide them – are effective and thoughtful ones.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Again, this is not a new point at all, it has been addressed and acknowledged in this House many times in the past.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, in the context of building inclusivity, I would like to re-emphasise the need to think about the digital experience as a whole and not just in respect of the functionality of specific services and apps.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us take a step back and consider for a moment – what does the larger digital environment look like right now, for a senior trying to live out their retirement years?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A number of bank branches have closed and self-service video teller machines have replaced human bank tellers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Medical appointments, prescription refills, health records – these are all accessible through apps such as HealthHub and Health Buddy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Shops, supermarkets and cafes have started to go cashless and smartphone apps are also used for the collection of points and allocation of discounts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If you go to a restaurant, chances are that you have to scan a QR code to access the menu and sometimes even to order and pay.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And while your entire life is condensed into your tiny smartphone, there is an additional fear and worry that you will be targeted by scammers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: All of these digital initiatives, while improving efficiency, do not necessarily improve overall experiences for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is perhaps easy to say that elderly folks unfamiliar with technological developments in banking, healthcare and other sectors should simply be educated on how to improve their digital skills or seek to depend on trusted family members for help.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, it overlooks the fact that not everyone has caregivers whom they can rely on.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For some of our seniors, doing their banking or shopping in person might be the only form of social interaction that they have in a single day.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: No one wants to feel like a burden or like they need re-education to just continue on with functions that they have managed independently for years.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While reported figures may indicate that more seniors are engaging in digital transactions, how many of these are in fact carried out by caregivers, friends or family members on their behalf?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There is a case to be made, I feel, for allowing seniors who wish to carry on with non-digital options to simply live out their lives as they wish in the way that they are used to.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They can learn to adopt digital solutions if they want, but they should be gradual and they should do this in their own time.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge that there are many good avenues for learning, such as the Seniors Go Digital initiative, and the Government has done well here.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But we must remember not to move too quickly.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This idea echoes a principle that can be found in the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights report entitled "Ensuring Access to Public Services in Digital Societies".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In this report, it says that while "member states should proactively support all initiatives by opening lifelong learning opportunities to older persons of all ages... individuals should not be obliged to acquire the necessary digital skills for access to digital services." The report then goes on to state that public administrations should always provide other access channels for citizens who cannot or do not want to acquire these skills.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Even if adaptability is required in a changing world, a positive choice needs to be made by a person to acquire new skills.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: His or her community then needs to provide the right environment for this learning to take place.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is, of course, not to say that we should all be Luddites who reject technological advances.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, there are many ways in which technology can be deployed to create inclusivity and safety for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's Digital Readiness Blueprint emphasises the need for user-centric design, which is absolutely spot on, but we need to remember to apply this thinking in an expansive way and not just in a piece-meal fashion.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We need to step into the shoes of our seniors in all the different demographics, seriously think through each of their respective lived experiences and apply our minds to how this technology can help them.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my second point, which is about how arts-related related initiatives can assist in building digital literacy, inclusivity and safety for our seniors in our digital society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Three examples come to mind, which I would like to share with you today.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, through the use of augmented reality (AR) technology, the gallery transformed more than 25 HDB void decks across heartland neighbourhoods into virtual art galleries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: All you had to do was point your phone camera at a QR code on a void deck wall and an artwork from the National Collection would appear before you as if it had been hung on that wall.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In one magical swoop, viewers could suspend physical reality for a moment and enjoy the experience of having a beautiful piece of art appear right in front of them.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They did not have to pay a single cent.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: All they had to do was simply turn on their phone cameras.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is technology which is easy to use and something that, to my mind, we could use just as easily in different scenarios, for example, in hospital waiting areas of geriatric clinics, where elderly folk are required to wait for lengthy periods of time.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These long waits can create huge amounts of stress for seniors whether they are alone or with caregivers and it is quite possible that access to digital art could alleviate some of that tension while familiarising our seniors with digital tools.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a great example of how technology can be inclusive, easily accessible and applied in a way that makes sense in order to serve the real needs of our seniors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The next example I would like to talk about is the use of technology in dementia care.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Artist and programmer Eugene Soh is one such person who is working in this space.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, he helps patients to cope with dementia using virtual reality (VR) technology.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They are also able to incorporate family members in created VR scenes, which helps the elderly patients to trigger memories, relieve social isolation and expand their physical boundaries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Being mindful of the fact that wearable VR goggles may not be attractive to seniors and may come with the risk of spreading viruses, Mind Palace decided to convert entire rooms into immersive interactive environments where interaction with fitness and meditative experiences is done via motion sensors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, to summarise, the whole experience is totally contactless and in line with what users of this service require and prefer.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is, again, another great example of solution-based and user-centric design thinking.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As Eugene described to me, his creativity is a compulsion.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is about using technology as a way of facilitating story-telling and expression, in a way that can reach out to communities in need in order to do some good.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Amongst others, the show featured an art piece that leveraged on face-swapping technology to show exhibition visitors how their images could be transformed into those of famous local celebrities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The point of this exhibit was to educate visitors about deepfake video call scams.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, the Government engages with popular creators on YouTube to raise awareness on scams and disseminates information through innovative mediums such as music videos.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud these steps and I hope that the Government takes note of our large arts community in Singapore and the talents that they have to offer.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Creative, entertaining and empathetic storytelling can result in much better outreach on digital literacy to different segments of society, including harder to reach groups like our seniors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While we progress in our Smart Nation goals towards inclusivity and safety, let us not forget these two points: first, that design thinking should always be applied in a holistic and empathetic manner to honour the full lived experiences of our seniors; and secondly, in our whole-of-nation Government strategies, especially when we think about the allocation of funding and other resources, let us not forget the important role that our artists and creatives play in crafting inclusivity and safety within our digital society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is notable that this trust extends to our institutions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is remarkable, considering an increasingly divided world where trust for state and government institutions is hard to come by.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have been able to maintain a high degree of trust between people, Government, organisations and businesses through many years of working and facing challenges together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this trust is fragile and can erode if our differences are manipulated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Racial or religious tensions, increasing income gaps, fake news, deepfakes, as shared by fellow Parliamentarian Dr Tan, perceived unfairness and unaddressed anxieties can very easily unravel the trust we have meticulously built over the years.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this Motion, our GPC thus calls for the House to reaffirm our commitment to adopt a whole-of-nation approach to sustain trust by building an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that amidst increased global digitalisation, everyone feels secure and feels part of our society?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we tackle falsehoods that threaten social cohesion?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we provide equal and equitable opportunities such that the opportunities do not only benefit the few at the top?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Redefining employment is essential as the employment landscape is evolving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The landscape is multifaceted and dynamic and any business owner in Singapore will tell you that we face challenges in securing the right manpower due to our limited population and an ageing demographic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It has been mentioned repeatedly that by 2030, one in four Singaporeans will be above the age of 60.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, jobs for seniors are typically manual in nature, such as cleaners and pump attendants, possibly because of the lack of digital skillset of the current seniors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, what is different compared to what we are experiencing now is our young seniors now are digitally literate and can continue to contribute to the economy in a different way.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At one of my house visits, I met a resident in her early 50s doing accounts for companies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She shared that since COVID-19, she has not been to her office.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She hopes that she can continue to do so, well into post-retirement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She wishes to continue working as she enjoys the interaction but wants to spend time with her grandchildren too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: COVID-19 has expedited the concept of flexible work arrangements in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Guidelines on flexible work arrangements have been shared by Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some degree of telecommuting is accepted as the norm at the workplace now.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, job sharing, staggered time, part-time work have yet to be embraced in earnest.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, how do we bring all of these different elements together and leverage digitalisation to meet the needs of our future seniors to have meaningful employment with a comfortable work-life balance when they retire, to meet the needs of future retirees to continue to build their retirement nest egg and to meet the manpower needs of our economy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To do so, we must take a structured, whole-of-nation approach to rethink the definition of employment to encourage flexible work arrangements like job sharing, staggered time, part-time work, where possible, to truly unlock the potential of digitally abled young seniors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, individuals with disabilities and back-to-work moms can stand to benefit too from such arrangements, helping to foster inclusivity while ensuring economic activity continues.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the grassroots level, we work with community partners to provide lower-income families with digital access.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This represents two out of every 100 households with kids in school still not having access to computers for whatsoever reason.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is worrying, especially when we consider that these households may likely be from the lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that all households with school-going children have access to computers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While ensuring connectivity and accessibility to digital devices is an undoubted priority, we must also ensure that our education system provides essential digital skills as early as at primary and secondary school levels.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After all, when Singapore pursued compulsory 10 years education, the intent is to ensure that our school-going children has the necessary basic knowledge and skills for their future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Typically, more affluent families send their kids to extra classes on coding, AI, AR and robotics.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The access to such expensive extra-curricular activities, especially at a young age, may not be available to the lower-income families who face hurdles in accessing resources as well as being aware of and learning these crucial digital skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This widens the skill gap between the haves and the have-nots.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure all our youths have equal opportunities to be exposed to and to develop these digital competencies?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I fear if we do not do so, kids from lower-income families are unduly disadvantaged in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it was reassuring to hear from Minister Chan Chun Sing yesterday, that MOE is preparing our students to develop the foundational knowledge of AI.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I hope we can have more digital skills taught formally in schools.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Providing a platform to create awareness and knowledge of the skills required in the digital economy, is precisely one of the things M3@PRPG (Pasir Ris-Punggol) hopes to achieve.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through our programs such as M3 goes digital, 3D Makers Workshop, Mentoring Program, Learning Journey and HashTech, M3@PRPG hopes to equip kids, especially those from the lower-income families with the awareness and basic knowledge of these skills and the possible opportunities in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Without such platforms, how will kids from lower-income families be aware of the skillsets required in the digital economy, let alone be inspired to have a career in these growing industries?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is only through trying that our students can cultivate their interest and aspire to continue doing it as a career.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Programmes such as M3 Does Digital and 3D Makers Space, where students learn about 3D printing; the M3 Learning Journey where students visit engineering and technology companies; and the #Hashtech programme where students pick up skills in dashboarding, cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence; all these provide a platform for our students to acquire digital skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One example is the champion of the 3D Makers Challenge.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The winning team comprises pupils from Madrasah Al-Arabiah Al-Islamiah who created a toy helicopter using 3D printing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another example is the runner-up in the #HashTech competition; a team of three siblings, Nurul Musfirah, Nurul Shahzanie and Nurul Zahirah, who presented an Artificial Intelligence (AI) platform that helps people to better understand the various support schemes currently available in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Congratulations to all the students and I would like to thank all volunteers from M3@Pasir Ris-Punggol, MENDAKI, MUIS, MAEC, MMiT dan MM in Engineering for giving our students the opportunity to improve their digital skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A few months ago, in my capacity as a panel member of the 4PM Bestari Award and Resilience Award for our youths studying at the ITE colleges, I was very moved when I saw the determination and resolve of these students in overcoming their challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of them are also pursuing further studies in various specialised fields, such as Applied AI and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To our students, please carry on pursuing digital knowledge.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our community must continue to encourage our students to explore and enhance their digital skills that are essential in the new economy. : Moving on from digital inclusion to the need to protect Singaporeans against online scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While many of our fellow Parliamentarians have talked about preventing scams, I will briefly touch on two post-scam recovery efforts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many scams originate from transactions which the victims have been misled to authorise.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, some scams are executed without the transactions being authorised.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, during the investigation, the victims' bank accounts or account, can be frozen.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can be highly challenging for the victims especially if it is the victim's sole account.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, trust remains delicate and will falter if left unnurtured.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Leveraging digital advancements responsibly is pivotal in sustaining trust within our communities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us collectively strive to build a safe, inclusive and trustworthy digital society where no one gets left behind.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While we are mindful of the challenges it presents, the benefits of embracing digital transformations are undeniable and pivotal for our nation's progress.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Digitalisation is a key driver of economic growth and innovation, opening doors to new markets and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It enhances operational efficiencies and productivity revolutionising how businesses operate and compete globally.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It empowers businesses to offer improved customer experiences, leveraging data analytics for more effective strategies and services.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While digitalisation can lead to the automation of some jobs, it also creates new ones.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Digitalisation also play a significant role in the environmental sustainability, reducing our carbon footprint through innovative solutions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The resilience demonstrated by businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic largely due to their digital capabilities, underscores the importance of being digitally prepared.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This readiness not only ensures business continuity in crises, but also strengthens our collective ability to adapt and thrive in changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore steadfastly progress towards our vision of a Smart Nation, it is imperative that our digital transformation journey is not only marked by technological advancement but is characterised by its inclusivity and safety.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This holistic approach is essential in ensuring that the benefits of digitalisation are accessible and secure for all members of our society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses are an important pillar of Singapore's digital society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many businesses are either adopting or developing digital products and services to better engage and serve the needs of consumers, and in a manpower tight situation, implementing digital solutions with automation to streamline operations to improve efficiencies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In an age where digital transactions and interactions are integral to our daily lives, the safety and security of digital information have become paramount concerns for users worldwide, including here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans are increasingly vigilant about how businesses handle their digital information.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Incidents like the SingHealth data breach in 2018, have left an indelible mark on the public consciousness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Another personal incident – a close friend of mine, who owns an engineering and construction company, experienced an ordeal that brings to light the stark realities of our digital age.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: His company was a victim of a ransomware attack, a malicious intrusion that stole his company servers and all of his engineering blueprints locked and encrypted by hackers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This attack brought his operations to a standstill with losses escalating every minute.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the financial toll extended beyond the ransom, with significant downtime and disruption losses adding to his burden.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Regrettably, his experience is not an isolated one that I know.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is a part of a growing trend of sophisticated cyber attacks that are deeply concerning the business community.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These incidents are stark reminders of the vulnerabilities in our digital infrastructure, the need for robust cybersecurity measures.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, in the face of a swiftly changing digital landscape, achieving digital inclusivity and safety necessitates significant investments in terms of finances, time and personnel.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This requirement may present considerable challenges to some companies, especially those with limited resources.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, businesses, regardless of their size, are grappling with challenges such as the need for upskilling staff to keep pace with technological advancements and a shortage of management expertise to effectively spearhead technological change.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While there is a growing confidence among businesses in managing cybersecurity challenges, with 80% feeling confident this year compared to 74% the previous year, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) still find themselves trailing behind their larger counterparts.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: According to recent data, 78% of SMEs feel confident or somewhat confident in their security measures to protect against cyber threats, which is lower compared to the 91% confidence level of larger companies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I aim to tackle the prevailing notion and apprehension among businesses, particularly small enterprises, that are implementing digital safety and cyber defences and feel that it is prohibitively expensive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I intend to introduce and discuss various tailored, accessible self-help tools and collaborative resources designed to enhance the cybersecurity stance of companies affordably and effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Internet Hygiene Portal (IHP), crafted by the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), serves as a comprehensive platform for businesses to utilise self-assessment tools.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These tools are designed to evaluate the security of a company's websites, email services and domain configurations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Following the assessment, IHP provides tailored, actionable recommendations, enabling companies to enhance their overall internet security posture effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the IHP enhances transparency by publishing an Internet Hygiene Rating table.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This feature offers a simplified overview of the cyber hygiene status of various digital platforms.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By providing such critical information, it empowers businesses and consumers alike to make informed decisions regarding their digital platform usage, therefore enhancing the security of their digital transactions and protecting against cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For SMEs who are ready to deepen their commitment to cybersecurity, CSA offers the Cybersecurity Health Plan.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Under this initiative, cybersecurity consultants act as the SMEs' virtual Chief Information Security Officers, conducting cyber health audits and crafting bespoke cybersecurity health plans.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Proper cyber risk management is pivotal for SMEs to confidently navigate their digitalisation journey.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The CTO-as-a-Service (CTOaaS) initiative, a part of the SMEs Go Digital Programme developed by IMDA and managed by SBF, is designed to bolster this confidence.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Through CTOaaS, SMEs gain access to a shared pool of seasoned digital consultants who provide comprehensive advisories and project management services.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This support helps SMEs identify and address digitalisation gaps and seize opportunities, ensuring a more secure and efficient digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs lacking in-house IT expertise or dedicated resources have found significant benefits in this service, receiving tailored digital solutions and training roadmaps specifically to their needs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative guarantees that SMEs have access to market-proven, cost-effective solutions, ensuring they are not marginalised in our collective stride towards an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is a step forward in democratising digital advancement, allowing all businesses, regardless of size or resource, to partake in and contribute to our digital future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Considering these existing initiatives, I would like to propose some recommendations to the Government to further support our SMEs: the development of resources tailored to the emerging and critical areas of digitalisation, such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence on a sector-specific basis.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By working closely with trade associations and companies, this approach can significantly accelerate SMEs' transition into an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These resources should encompass sector-specific training and assessment plans, baseline tools, and solutions that are pertinent to each industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Also, as highlighted in the recent Singapore Business Federation (SBF)-KPMG Budget recommendations for 2024, the Government can consider adjusting existing grant schemes to support SMEs in adopting these tools and solutions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This comprehensive strategy will not only safeguard our businesses but also empower them to confidently embrace the digital future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As technology becomes even more integral in our daily lives, the demand for skilled workers correspondingly evolves.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential to cultivate a culture of learning and innovation within our workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As leaders and stakeholders, we must recognise and address the apprehensions of our workers, providing reassurance and support to those who may feel overwhelmed by the rapid digital changes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must continue to invest significantly in training our workers, ensuring that every individual, regardless of their starting point, is given the opportunity to grow and adapt.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is not just about keeping pace with the digital society; it is about empowering them to lead and innovate within it.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By fostering continuous learning, providing comfort and guidance, and encouraging innovation, we would not only enhance individual careers but also drive the collective progress of our industries and the nation as a whole.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore crucial for companies to recognise that training our workforce transcends merely keeping pace with technological advancements; it is also about strategically upskilling them to unlock the full potential of technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When our workers are adept and agile, the company as a whole reaps substantial benefits.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, Utracon Corporation, through its participation in the CTOaaS initiative, leveraged expert advice to implement targeted solutions, significantly enhancing real-time project monitoring and fostering improved team collaboration.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This example underscores the broader value of investing in our employees' growth, leading to enhanced operational efficiency and innovative capabilities within the company.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is a fundamental aspect of building trust and maintaining the integrity of our businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   In conclusion, as we navigate the complexities and opportunities of building an inclusive and safe digital society, let us embrace a holistic approach.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This involves not only investing in robust technology and infrastructure, but also fostering a culture of continuous learning, innovation and ethical practice.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we ensure that our journey towards a Smart Nation is one marked by trust, security and inclusivity, benefiting every individual and business within our society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Together, let us commit to a future where digital advancement equates to a safer, more prosperous and ethically grounded Singapore for all. : Mr Speaker Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the last few years, the Government and key players in society have kept up with and utilised technology to make our lives better and simpler.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Once upon a time, each of us had to keep physical copies of all our important documents, including birth certificates, identity cards, driver's licences, health records, marriage certificates, bank account statements and CPF statements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, all this information is readily available on or through apps on our mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Singpass app readily links us to most of our official records, while all major banks provide most of their services through mobile phone apps.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For many of us, there is probably no need to carry cash or wallets anymore, or to queue up at post offices, banks, ATM or AXS machines, as almost all payments can be done on our phones, from wherever we are.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even the marketing and shopping experience has changed completely, with online stores now bringing this experience to our fingertips.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We can now shop from the comfort of home or while on public transport.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, when I spoke to an executive in an online retailer, she mentioned that very significant percentage of shoppers made purchases while they were in the toilet in the morning.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These changes have also changed our business landscape significantly, with online giants such as Amazon and Alibaba replacing physical retailers such as Borders and Robinsons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For small businesses, getting goods displayed on platforms like Shopee and Lazada allows them to sell without retail shopfronts, while for those who have retail shopfronts, getting online has been an important way to supplement sales.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Motion highlights two important issues that need to be addressed in this move to digitisation: inclusion and safety.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those of us who are online and get our services online, life has never been easier.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For young people too, getting online seems to be second nature.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My daughter had learnt to download games on my wife's mobile phone from around the age of four or five, and shortly after that, she had learnt to make online purchases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All this, without any of us teaching her.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, I do have many older residents who are not fully online and struggle.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I used to get requests for more bank branches to remain open when banks started closing branches and transitioning people to ATMs and AXS machines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, banks are also pulling back on ATMs and residents who have spent a lifetime transacting with cash are now finding it more difficult to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The same applies to many small business owners, and while many shops in wet markets and HDB malls have gone digital, there are still a few who have not signed on to online payments or record keeping.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes some very educated people, including, in some cases, senior doctors who prefer to practice the way they have done for many years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There have been wide ranging initiatives by different Government agencies to bridge this divide and bring more people into the digital fold.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe these initiatives are working, but in order for them to work better, I think it will take the whole of society to be involved, for us to encourage people around us to go for courses, go online and become more enabled.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Whenever I get requests by residents for more ATMs, I explain the challenges we face in getting more ATMs, but also gently nudge them to getting online banking apps and to move digital.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next aspect of the Motion which has received a lot of attention is digital security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes keeping systems operating and protecting from cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There have been several instances, for example, of some of our banking systems going down, preventing transactions taking place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Where people operate largely digitally, this can create issues.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, if a bank's payment systems are down, what happens to people who only have digital means of payment from that bank?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I suffered a minor inconvenience in this because I was at a shop the first time the system went down.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had to return the items and went back home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Not a major issue but definitely something that needs to be looked at if we are going more digital.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But more important are malicious cyber threats, including hacking and ransomware, where organisations may have systems hacked, information stolen and then demands are made for payment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many companies and organisations have extensive personal information from individuals and if the systems on which these are stored are not secured, individuals could be exposed to attacks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On these matters, I think it is necessary to ensure that those who collect personal data are able to protect it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third aspect which I think has received the most attention from many speakers in this House is online scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have spoken on this issue several times in this House.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This makes it difficult for local law enforcement agencies to take action against them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, victims normally have their trust taken advantage of.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The types of scams include job scams, love scams and investment scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some in this House have spoken about how the prevalence of scams is creating a crisis of confidence in our digitisation process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think digitisation is a fast moving train and most Singaporeans are on board.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The victims of scams are often too trusting and take at face value the calls and messages they get, which hook them into the process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the course of my work, I was approached by a victim of a love scam.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: She had fallen in love with an individual through online exchanges and one meeting in-person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Eventually, this individual allegedly died, leaving her a massive inheritance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, to get this inheritance, she had to and did make regular payments for various purportedly official purposes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is still difficult for her to believe she has been scammed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: She still wants to believe there is an inheritance waiting for her.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Scammers are essentially criminals who are trying to steal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Digitisation has simply created an easier way for them to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think there is a crisis of confidence in digitisation, but rather this is a matter on which each consumer must learn to be more careful and vigilant.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Just as in the real world, we take precautions, such as not leaving our wallets and phones lying around, or leaving our houses unlocked when we are out, we must exercise the same care digitally.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third challenge is where the losses for these scams should fall.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, we are all sympathetic to the victim, who have been taken advantage of.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some have lost life savings or monies they needed for important purposes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of the victims I have met at the Meet-the-People Sessions have had heart wrenching stories.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are calls for more of these losses to fall on telco operators and/or banks, or generally, any other big companies that may be involved in this process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We all believe that big companies should be better able to bear losses than individuals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We also want to put more pressure on big companies to take the necessary precautions to protect individuals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would, however, like to highlight some risks I see if we swing too far in this direction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, every large company, including banks and telcos, have to make money from their customers and if taking a large proportion of losses from online scams falls on them, they will have to recoup these losses from one of their customers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, we may see prices rising across the board.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, this may mean that more invasive approaches by service providers to their customers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, if telcos are held liable for scams through phone calls or WhatsApp messages, they probably going to have to take more efforts to monitor and scan private calls and messages in order to ferret out scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To what extent do we want banks to second guess instructions and transactions?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third point, that of moral hazard, has been recognised.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If people believe that losses may fail elsewhere, they are more likely to take less precaution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think many of us already have this adopted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) have also begun working with banks to tackle this issue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: MAS has also been involved in this approach to combat scams, working closely with banks to strengthen anti-malware controls, faults surveillance and detection capabilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Major retail banks have enhanced their security measures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, certainly, bigger organisations and the Government are taking steps to fight scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, the most important approach is the third aspect, which is public education.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think SPF, Cyber Security Agency, MoneySENSE and banks have used multiple platforms, reach out to residents and many of us, Members of Parliament, have also been conducting talks and dialogues in our constituencies to encourage people to download ScamShield and to warn them about the risks of scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is also involved and plugged into global cooperation to fight scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have to play our part if we want others to assist us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There was a recent crackdown in Singapore where large numbers of people were arrested and I believe a large part of this money is from crimes committed abroad.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, the full details of this are large scale arrests and seizure methods have not been released, but I think it is part of our cooperation with international work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a matter that affects all countries and other countries like the UK, Australia and the United States and also similarly taking these approaches to fight scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
