text: One initiative that caught my attention was actually "Stop Scams UK", which is an industry led collaboration of businesses, including major banks, credit card operators and big online players, such as Amazon and Google.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the UK, just like in Singapore, fraud is the most commonly experienced crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the UK, one is twice as likely to be the victim of a fraud than any other crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is where a payee poses as someone else and defrauds victims to make payment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: By placing potential lability on private sector players, they have been financially incentivised to get together to work to stop APP scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even they are not ambitious or claiming that it can be completely eradicated but they just want to reduce the incidence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is something that is going to be with us, but with which we all have to take the necessary precautions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, it may be necessary for the Government to take the lead in these initiatives and/or in the passed legislation, to put adequate risk for industry players.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe that financially aligned industry collaboration is, in general, a sensible approach.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have to embrace and ride this wave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Members may also access the handout through the MP@SG Parl mobile app.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Mark Lee asked about the impact of digitalisation, especially the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on our workforce and our SMEs and our businesses.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The field of AI, generative AI, in particular, is evolving rapidly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Analysts' predictions on the impact of AI on the workforce and industries vary greatly and sometimes, even contradict each other.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But there is broad consensus that AI is here and its development will have profound effects on the world and the certainly for us on this little red dot.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We should not be overly fearful or be overly anxious of this trend.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Instead, we should confidently embrace the possibilities with AI.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The competition is not between "man" and "machine" but which economy and society can better use technology to improve our competitiveness and our lives.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Singapore is well placed to harness the power of AI, as we have done in previous waves of technological change.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government's approach has always been to support our businesses and workers to adapt to changes so that they can fully benefit from the opportunities that digital technologies can bring.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government will continue to work with our tripartite partners, including our Labour unions on this important effort as suggested by Ms Jean See, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Mark Lee.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Dr Wan Rizal raised the issue of the impact of technology on mental health and well-being.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This House will have a fuller discussion on this topic during the Motion on "Advancing Mental Health" next month.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, let me just broadly touch on MCI's approach on this issue.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MCI recognises that technology and social media use can have grave impact on mental health and well-being.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As Dr Wan Rizal, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum, Ms Nadia Samdin as well as Ms Mariam Jaafar had mentioned, such risks include exposure to harmful online content, such as cyberbullying and self-harm content, as well as excessive and problematic use of social media.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To mitigate these risks to Singaporean users, MCI has introduced regulatory measures to enhance online safety for users, which Minister Josephine Teo will touch on later.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We also work with partners across the public, private and people sectors to raise awareness amongst Singaporeans on online safety and good practices on using technology in a healthy and balanced manner.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, we work with the Ministry of Education (MOE) to strengthen cyber wellness education in schools, teaching students to be discerning, safe, respectful and responsible users of the online space.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They are also taught the importance of respect and empathy, how they can protect themselves and others online and to seek help when necessary.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Dr Wan Rizal also spoke about the role of parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We agree that parents play a crucial role in guiding their children's digital journey, especially at the early stages.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We work with partners, such as the Media Literacy Council, to develop resources for parents and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MCI has also worked with technology companies to launch an Online Safety Digital Toolkit in March last year, which guides parents to make use of the parental controls, privacy and reporting tools, as well as self-help resources on the social media platforms.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Collectively, these efforts aim to make the online space safer for all and empower individuals with the know-how to protect themselves and their loved ones and it is an ongoing journey.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will continue to work with partners in this effort.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Members have made many good points on how digitalisation has brought benefits and opportunities to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Indeed, as a little red dot with scarce natural resources, we cannot afford to unplug from the global digital economy, especially when others are actively pursuing strategies to be more digital, including leveraging emerging technologies like AI.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Therefore, our aim has always been to make digital work for all so that every Singaporean can benefit.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I am glad that all Members share this belief.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Ong Hua Han and Ms Usha Chandradas spoke about some of the challenges that Singaporeans face when going digital.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I meet many Singaporeans in similar circumstances in my walkabouts, Meet-the-People Sessions as well as many focus groups.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Making digital work for all is not just about going digital, but also recognising that some Singaporeans still prefer non-digital options for certain transactions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Our approach is therefore not digital only for all.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: An example is CDC Vouchers, which Ms Jessica Tan mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I believe most Singaporeans claimed their CDC Vouchers digitally.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, those who prefer to use physical vouchers can visit Community Centres to print hard copy vouchers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To better support residents, student volunteers, Silver Infocomm Wellness Ambassadors and our Digital Ambassadors are on hand to help.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Singaporeans who need in-person support for Government services can visit one of our seven ServiceSG Centres.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Centres can help with close to 600 Government services and schemes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Making digital work for all also means supporting all Singaporeans, regardless of their circumstances, to benefit from digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is often said that the measure of a society is how it looks after its most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are taking steps to support those who need more help to benefit from going digital.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In this regard, we are building on a solid foundation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Last year, IMDA released the inaugural Singapore Digital Society report as a stocktake of our efforts.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have made good progress over the years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are one of the most digitally connected countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Our digital inclusion efforts are well regarded internationally.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Singapore has ranked first on the Inclusive Internet Index from 2018, to the latest report released in 2022.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These datapoints show that we are on the right track.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But we are not resting on our laurels.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Sharael Taha stressed the importance of supporting lower-income households with digital connectivity.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In particular, together with preceding schemes like NEU PC Plus, we have supported a total of 26,000 households with school-going children with access to digital devices over the last three years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Currently, 98% of resident households with school-going children have computer access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will continue to support the remaining 2% through schemes like DigitalAccess@Home.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This complements efforts by MOE and schools to support students' home-based learning by providing school-prescribed personal learning devices to secondary school students under the National Digital Literacy Programme.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In addition, schools loan computers and internet-enabling devices to students who require them for school work.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will continue to work with schools and our community partners to reach out to all families with school-going children.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We also introduced the Mobile Access for Seniors scheme in June 2020 to provide lower-income seniors with subsidised smartphones and mobile data plans along with training.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Since 2020, over 11,000 lower-income seniors have benefited.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Importantly, industry and community partners play a big part to support digital access for lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, SG Bono, a non-profit organisation refurbishes donated laptops for use by lower-income families, especially those with school-going children.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I am particularly glad to know that SG Bono extended this support to madrasah students from lower-income households since 2021.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is another group of microbusinesses or Singaporeans that we are supporting through the Hawkers Go Digital programme.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As of November last year, more than 11,000 stallholders, which is around 60% of all hawkers, have adopted e-payments via the Singapore Quick Response Code (SGQR) platform.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In addition to SGQR and e-payments, this digitalisation support to hawkers and heartland merchants give them the confidence to come onboard other digital initiatives such as the CDC Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I am very encouraged to see many stories of how these heartland merchants and small businesses have further built on this foundation and gone further to transform their business models and capture the opportunities of e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Ong Hua Han and others spoke about the Seniors Go Digital programme and asked about the progress.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Seniors Go Digital programme was set up to equip seniors with basic digital skills so that they too can be part of a digital society and enjoy the benefits of going digital.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the time of the programme's inception in 2020, the need was particularly pressing with the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Since then, we have conducted training for over 280,000 seniors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Uptick in seniors' adoption of digital skills has improved over time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, in 2022, 86% of seniors knew how to find information online, a 29% increase from just three years ago in 2019.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I am always inspired by our seniors who gamely picked up digital skills even though it can be challenging at the outset.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is a testament to their spirit of lifelong learning and the dedication of SDO's Digital Ambassadors, our Silver Infocomm Wellness Ambassadors as well as family and friends who patiently guide seniors on their digitalisation journey.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Singaporeans who want to learn digital skills can visit one of the 37 SG Digital Community Hubs islandwide and they can visit one of the more than 200 roving counters in our workplaces, healthcare institutions and community spaces.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Another aspect is designing services inclusively, with the needs of specific groups in mind.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Nadia Samdin and Mr Ong Hua Han spoke about supporting persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In particular, I would like to thank Mr Ong for his feedback on behalf of the deaf and the visually impaired communities, and for his thoughtful suggestions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are making progress towards our goal of making all high traffic Government websites fully accessible to persons with disabilities by 2030.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have increased the percentage of high traffic Government websites which are fully accessible from 61% in 2022 to 73% last year.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Ong Hua Han mentioned that we have introduced sign language interpretation for key national events and critical public announcements to improve access to information of national importance.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Nadia Samdin raised the importance of supporting persons with disabilities with assistive technology and learning digital skills.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The fund can be used to acquire, replace, upgrade or repair those devices.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They can also receive assessment and training in the use of these devices at Tech Able, which is an assistive technology centre jointly managed by SG Enable and the disability social service agency, SPD, at the Enabling Village.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Digital Enablement Programme, which Ms Nadia Samdin mentioned, is a Digital for Life (DfL)-funded programme which supports persons with disabilities with essential digital skills for a world of hybrid work.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As of March 2023, the programme has supported 200 training places.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I agree with Mr Ong Hua Han that industry partners, especially those providing essential services, must play their part to enhance the accessibility of their services.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are lowering the adoption barriers for industry partners through providing resources and tools.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: SG Enable provides e-accessibility training and consultancy services for companies to learn how e-accessibility features can be incorporated into their digital services.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The GovTech Accessibility Enabling Team (ALLY) has developed Purple ALLY, a free and open-sourced testing tool for digital teams to check how they can make their digital products or services more accessible.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Ong also asked if we can ensure that future digital infrastructure designers and programmers are exposed to digital accessibility.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will continue to work with our Institutes of Higher Learning on this.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, students in the Diploma in Design at Ngee Ann Polytechnic design electronic devices to support users with disabilities as part of their curriculum.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will continue to work with Institutes of Higher Learning to incorporate some of these considerations into their curriculum.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I encourage industry partners to make use of these resources and do more to make their services accessible to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, I commend the spirit of Mr Ong's remarks and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: All of us, as a society, can do more to make our digital services and products more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As a first step, it is oftentimes understanding where each other is coming from and how we can take pragmatic steps to achieve that.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In that regard, I would certainly love to invite Mr Ong to address and speak to many of our community partners on this aspect.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government cannot do this on our own.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I am glad many Members – Ms Hany Soh, Mr Ong Hua Han, Ms Usha Chandradas and others – emphasised that this is a whole-of-nation effort.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government, corporates, communities and individuals must come together to support different groups who need help on their journeys.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Digital for Life movement launched in 2021 is an important part of this collective effort.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And it is making encouraging progress, bringing together three key partners – the public sector, private sector and people sector – for this common cause.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Partners have also come forward to generously contribute some $14 million to the DfL Fund, which supports digital inclusion efforts, including ground-up projects from the community.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I am heartened that there are many who are willing to step forward to support their fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I encourage more partners to step forward and work together with us.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, Ms Usha shared examples of how we can better involve members of the arts community in our digital inclusion effort.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: After all, what good is connectivity and a digital device if we do not have the skills to use them for our benefit?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar spoke about AI literacy and Mr Sharael Taha spoke about how we must give all Singaporeans, especially students from lower-income families, opportunities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOE launched the Transforming Education through Technology plan in September last year to further strengthen students' development of digital literacy and technological skills, starting with AI literacy.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Yesterday, MOE has also responded to questions from Members on opportunities for our students to learn about AI.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Together with MOE, we introduced the Code For Fun (CFF) programme to expose students to coding and computational thinking.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Since 2020, it has been mandatory for all upper primary school students to go through CFF or a comparable coding programme.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As technology continues to evolve, IMDA and MOE will review the CFF enrichment programme to ensure that it is relevant and up to date.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are working towards introducing new content on AI and data literacy in the refreshed curriculum for 2025.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Outside schools, there are many opportunities for students, young people and members of the public to explore new technology.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For instance, community partners like SGBono and VIVITA have been collaborating with the Bedok Social Service Office to bring tech experiences closer to children from less privileged backgrounds who typically would not have such opportunities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Earlier, Members raised many good initiatives in the community.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For the general public, we have programmes like ExperienceIT and MakeIT at our libraries.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These showcase emerging technologies and innovations, such as AI, machine learning and 3D printing, through informative displays and hands-on activities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, please check out these exhibits and showcases at your nearest library.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, we recognise that some of us may not be ready to take on the more advanced digital skills.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We may want to focus first on building the fundamentals to go online safely and use digital services and tools confidently in our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In the handout distributed, Members will find a factsheet with more details on DSL.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Unlike existing frameworks to equip Singaporeans with digital skills for the workplace or specific sectors, DSL outlines the digital skills to enable Singaporeans to carry out day-to-day tasks online.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have referenced overseas examples and got inputs from experts.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Through the Internet, we can access limitless information and new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But we need to know how to search, view and retrieve this information safely for our use.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Fourthly, transacting online for greater convenience – accessing banking and Government services, booking healthcare appointments, just to name a few examples.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And importantly, fifth, being safe, smart and kind online – understanding how to keep ourselves safe from scams and false information and how to build a positive presence online.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These are all practical skills that can make a real difference to Singaporeans' day-to-day lives.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: A few years ago, I met an elderly lady at the SG Digital Community Hub at Heartbeat@Bedok.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: She was asking our Digital Ambassador many questions on how to use her smartphone and I saw her taking copious notes down on a small, little notepad.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: She was probably around her late fifties and early sixties, speaking in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When I asked what she was learning, her answer both surprised and inspired me.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: She said that she was a victim of an online scam and she lost some money.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: She was there to learn how to make sure that this would not happen to her again.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, instead of being fearful and withdrawing, she wanted to confront the issue head on by learning how to safeguard herself.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Digital Ambassador at the Hub patiently walked her through practical cybersecurity tips that would be useful for all of us.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, how to create a stronger password instead of just using the default password "Password" which scammers could easily guess.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I was most heartened by her resilient spirit and willingness to learn, and we want to support Singaporeans like her with the right tools, resources and competencies to pick up the skills they need.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To do so, we are collaborating with partners under the DfL movement to develop resources in line with the DSL framework.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Interested learners can access in-person learning at the SG Digital Community Hubs where Digital Ambassadors and Silver Infocomm Wellness Ambassadors will walk alongside less-digitally savvy Singaporeans on their journeys.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Learners can also learn at your own pace and access videos and guidebooks on the Digital for Life Portal.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Those who are keen to help their family and friends pick up skills can use these resources to teach them.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is a small contribution to the global digitalisation process.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Our partners can refer to these resources when conducting digital skills training.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They can also use innovative ways to help learning and further promote the DSL movement.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, turning materials into games to make children's learning more interesting and vivid, or creating audio and video content in dialects to introduce the five basic skills to the elderly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I hope that everyone will make good use of these resources to benefit more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The DSL framework is a starting point to help Singaporeans embark on their digital journey.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Just as we start learning to write by mastering each stroke, acquiring digital skills must also start from the very basic level.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: With a solid foundation, as digital technology advances, we will be more confident in learning new skills and keeping up with the times.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will regularly review this framework to ensure that the content it covers meets our current needs. : Let me conclude.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Over the years we have made great strides to build our vision of an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In our physical world, we are comfortable to let our loved ones walk freely down the street, trusting that they will have pleasant interactions with people and not have to look over their shoulders for threats.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But it is all up to us to keep our digital streets safe.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When the Smart Nation Initiative was launched in 2014, we envisioned Singapore as "a nation where people live meaningful and fulfilled lives, enabled seamlessly by technology, offering exciting opportunities for all." A decade on, this vision has certainly come alive.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Technology has become a big part of our daily lives and 84% of Singaporeans say they have benefited in one way or another.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Although they represent just over 5% of all jobs, there are thousands more across all other sectors that have been enhanced by digital technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our aim must be for all Singaporeans to gain from these developments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How has spoken about digital inclusion and the Government's efforts to ensure that benefits are felt by all segments of society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, our digital way of life has exposed us to new risks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cyberattacks, scams and harmful content pose a growing threat to our safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As many Members have noted, trust in society, so crucial for normal human interactions, could be undermined.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will focus my speech on two topics specifically.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first is what we have we done so far to protect Singaporeans in the digital domain; and the second, what more we need to keep people safe.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unfortunately, in the digital domain, there are few ready playbooks with proven solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, Singapore is considered an early mover in digital governance and has been recognised as such.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Mark Lee spoke about the need for our businesses to protect and handle customer information ethically.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We moved to address this issue more than a decade ago.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2012, we introduced the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), before the EU's General Data Protection Regulation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By 2020, we had amended the Act to strengthen organisational accountability and consumer protection, while bolstering confidence for using personal data for innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2018, we enacted the Cybersecurity Act to address the threats in cyberspace, particularly those faced by our critical information infrastructure (CII).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Beyond protecting our CII, we have also introduced initiatives to help businesses enhance their cybersecurity posture.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Also, I had previously announced that we expect to update the Cybersecurity Act so that it remains fit-for-purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Public consultations on the proposed amendments are ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2019, recognising the harms of misinformation, we introduced the Prevention of Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a small, multiracial, and multi-religious country, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to falsehoods that deepen fault lines and polarise society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: POFMA is a calibrated tool to safeguard the infrastructure of fact.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Its usefulness was especially evident during the COVID-19 pandemic, to defend against all kinds of falsehoods about vaccines and COVID-19 related deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2021, to counter potential hostile information campaigns launched by other states against us, we introduced the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act (FICA).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This helps to ensure that Singapore politics remains only for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dr Wan Rizal, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Nadia Samdin spoke about the risks of children being exposed to harmful content online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also introduced measures to tackle this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In July 2023, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) launched the Code of Practice for Online Safety.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It requires social media services with significant reach or impact in Singapore to put in place measures to minimise users' exposure to harmful content on their platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include additional measures to protect children below-18 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dr Rizal and Ms Nadia suggested that platforms implement age assurance measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is currently no foolproof measure to prevent false age declarations on social media platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, age assurance is achievable to a fairly high degree of accuracy without compromising privacy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MCI and IMDA are monitoring the developments and will study viable regulatory options to better protect children online through age assurance measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am aware that Mr Darryl David will speak about addressing online dangers such as cyber stalking and body shaming, and providing support for victims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, online harassment and doxxing are dealt with under the Protection from Harassment Act 2014.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Victims can seek redress through the Protection from Harassment Court, which has served thousands since it was set up in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Ministry of Law (MinLaw) is looking further into how victims can be better empowered to put a stop to such online harms, and to seek redress from those responsible.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MinLaw's efforts will complement MCI's efforts to enhance the Government's regulatory tool kit, as well as the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)'s efforts to address online criminal harms, which I will say more about later.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have consciously avoided a big-bang approach, choosing instead an accretive approach to understand the issues deeply and to move quickly when we identify measures that are likely to be effective.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where solutions are untested, we have not held back completely.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, we have introduced model frameworks or advisory guidelines for voluntary adoption.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also developed practical tools to help organisations meet their regulatory obligations, or raised governance standards.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will remain Singapore's approach to digital governance for the foreseeable future.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It was, in fact, how we dealt with AI governance.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More recently, we committed to develop Advisory Guidelines on the use of personal data in AI systems, including safeguards to protect personal data of vulnerable groups like children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore will continue to participate actively at international fora, such as the Global Partnership on AI and the United Nations' High Level Advisory Board on AI.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As mentioned by Ms Tan and Ms Mariam, we have refreshed our AI strategies through NAIS 2.0.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will soon update our recommendations on dealing with AI risks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, we are very concerned about the mis-use of generative AI to spread misinformation and carry out targeted scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Of all the risks in the digital domain, one category is particularly concerning – and they are scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This was an issue raised by almost all MPs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Recent concerns about scams may sound new, but are in fact very similar to past cases of fraud.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Older Singaporeans may remember the sale of fake insurance policies in the 1970s.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2006, Sunshine Empire, which disguised itself as a multi-level marketing company, operated a Ponzi Scheme that promised high returns on fake products and services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the early 2010s, the SureWin4U Ponzi Scheme lured victims to invest in betting schemes against casinos.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These days, scammers use technology to sell fake jobs, fake love and fake discounted items like eggs or holiday packages.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Through variety, speed and scale, they have claimed more victims than before.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Whenever I speak with a scam victim and hear their harrowing experience, I am reminded of a very similar panic I experienced as a child.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Back in the 1970s, I lived with my grandmother in an old shophouse in Joo Chiat.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On several occasions, we were awakened in the middle of the night to nearby shouts of "Fire!

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We had very little clue as to how far and fast the fire might reach us, only that we must be ready to run for our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This kind of fear and helplessness, you never forget.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, fire hazards have largely been brought under control and most fire incidents have moderate impact.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is because we have well-trained and well-equipped firefighters to contain fires that do break out.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are regulations, including the Fire Safety Code, to prevent potential fire incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also have the support of organisations and citizens alike, who do their part to create and maintain an environment safe from fires.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In many ways, we are fighting scams like how we successfully fought fires.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have invested resources to strengthen our capabilities to contain the impact of emerging scam campaigns.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Two years ago, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) established the Anti-Scam Command (ASCom).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This helps to facilitate the swift tracing of funds and freezing of scam-tainted bank accounts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also put in place tools to limit losses for victims, much like the use of retardants to slow the spread of fires.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Banks have implemented an emergency "kill-switch", so customers can quickly suspend their accounts if they suspect compromise.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In November last year, several banks implemented a "Money Lock" feature, allowing customers to set aside an amount in their bank accounts that cannot be transferred digitally.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another recent example is the lower default daily limit for online CPF withdrawals, which cannot be increased without strong user authentication.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members can also disable online CPF withdrawals easily by activating the CPF Withdrawal Lock, which instantly reduces this limit to $0.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Preventive safeguards are easier said than done, as they require close coordination with industry.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Several sets of measures have been or are being implemented.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, we will keep closing off known avenues for scammers to reach prospective victims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will recall that not too long ago, scammers were spoofing the SMS IDs of key organisations to trick victims into giving their banking credentials.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To counter this, IMDA introduced a novel solution.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: From January last year, all organisations that want to send SMSes using alphanumeric sender IDs had to register with the Singapore SMS Sender ID Registry (SSIR).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SMSes from unregistered senders are labelled "Likely-SCAM" to alert phone users.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cases of scam SMSes fell by 70% in the first three months that it was mandated and remain a minority – less than 5% – among new cases reported.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Additionally, telcos have implemented firewalls within their networks to proactively block suspicious calls and calls that attempt to spoof local numbers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To further protect the public, telcos have now introduced an option for subscribers to block their mobile phones from receiving international calls, which is a common source of scam calls.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As mentioned by Mr Ong, scammers are increasingly abusing online platforms to deceive their potential victims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many Members supported the Bill and I thank them again.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This Act will allow authorities to order the swift blocking of online accounts or content suspected to be used for crimes, including scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For the protection of consumer on high-risk platforms, we will also impose ex-ante requirements such as stricter requirements for identity verification.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second set of preventive safeguards aim to disrupt fraudulent transactions, even after a victim has been tricked.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes preventing Singpass accounts from being taken over.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is why last year, we introduced more friction into the authentication process for Singpass.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When conducting high-risk transactions, users are required to perform facial verification.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To protect against impersonation attempts, which Ms Hazel Poa asked about, facial verification includes liveness checks, which guards against attacks such as using a still photo.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Facial verification was also introduced as an additional safeguard for high-risk CPF e-services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Also last year, we observed the emergence of scammers exploiting malware to bypass existing safeguards and make unauthorised fraudulent transactions on victims' accounts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Having identified this new scam variant, we worked with the banks to enhance their fraud and malware detection capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Compromised devices were prevented from transacting with the banks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We cannot quantify it but millions more dollars could otherwise have been lost.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ultimately, our devices themselves must be better able to defend against malware attacks launched by scammers – Ms Tin spoke about this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are therefore working with key industry players to enhance the security of mobile devices sold in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For instance, we are working with Google to design new features that can better detect and deter users from downloading malicious files onto Android devices.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third set of measures involve harsher consequences to deter money mules from misusing our key digital services, such as Singpass, to perpetrate scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have recently tightened our legislation to criminalise individuals who intentionally disclose their Singpass credentials in aid of scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are also reviewing how to extend these principles to those who sell SIM cards to scammers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Tan spoke about the need for platform players, telcos and device manufacturers to do more to improve online safety for their users.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As mentioned by Mr Ong and Mr Tan, we need companies to ensure that their customers can enjoy a safe and secure environment as they interact online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last August, OCBC was among the first banks in Singapore to disallow account access, if the bank app detected the presence of potentially risky mobile apps on the customers' devices.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some customers felt inconvenienced, but in fact, they may have been among those that were saved from at least $2 million in losses in the first month of roll-out.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The MAS has since worked with other major banks to implement similar safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During the public consultation on the SRF, many suggestions were received, which are similar to those raised today.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They relate to the expansion of coverage to more scam types and more entities, besides banks and telcos.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The SRF covers phishing scams because such scams were the main contributor to fraudulent transactions taking place without the consumer's knowledge and consent when SRF was first conceived.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Compared to the payout frameworks in other jurisdictions, which only impose obligations on banks, the SRF already holds a wider scope of entities accountable by including telcos.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Duties are also specified to clearly hold banks and telcos accountable to the victims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even if there is no breach of duty and, hence, no payout under SRF, there are other avenues of recourse for victims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include banks' goodwill frameworks, which can provide some comfort to victims of new scam tactics.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As was shared in Parliament last year, MAS has leaned on the banks to be more accommodative in applying their goodwill frameworks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These complementary measures notwithstanding, the Government will consider how to enhance the accountability of key entities and strengthen protection for individuals within SRF or through other means that are available to us.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We hear the specific calls to include social media platforms and closed-messaging services, in particular, for scam variants involving malware and phishing that result in unauthorised transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I appreciate Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Hazel Poa's acknowledgment that there are trade-offs and moral hazards to consider and that the Government cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With regard to physical tokens, these are available upon customer request.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I should caution, however, that existing physical tokens may be resistant to malware, but they are still vulnerable to phishing tactics.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Mr Yip Hon Weng's suggestion to learn from best practices abroad, we have been proactive.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many measures have also reduced the losses – stemmed the losses – to a very significant extent.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, then that begs the question, "What about these rankings that you come across that named Singapore as one of these top places in terms of how much victims have lost?" Well, I can only say this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In many places, scam victims are not going to take the trouble to report the fact that they have been scammed, because they do not expect whichever authority they report to, to be able to do anything about it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And so, when these kinds of reports are a function of reporting, what this really tells us is that reporting levels in Singapore are very high.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is, of course, not to trivialise the amounts lost.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But I think we have to recognise that fact.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this regard, I think we also have to recognise that our members of the public have been quite remarkable in terms of their openness and willingness to pay attention to public education efforts on scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I appreciate that it sometimes makes them quite anxious – because they keep hearing about it when they are at the bus stop, they see it when they are at the void deck and they see the digital display panels and then they go to a grassroots event and the Member of Parliament is also advising them to listen to the Police talk about anti-scam measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But it is an essential part of our overall scam defence which we cannot avoid and which we aim to fortify through a variety of means.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And so, the question is: what more can we do?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, let us take a step back and acknowledge that all countries recognise that when it comes to dealing with scams, there is really no silver bullet.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is not a single measure that you can implement and be done with it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the trade, they call this a wicked problem.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In cyber as well as in scams, you solve one problem, the bad actors are driven somewhere else and you have to start again.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, an agile approach is critical and a very good example is how we had to very quickly pivot to dealing with the malware-enabled scams which had not been conceived of before and had not been seen before.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is very easy to say that, "You should have anticipated it." Not so easy in reality.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The last thing, in this context, is not for us to politicise the debate or to vilify any group because you do not know when the next scam variant comes around who you need to work with to try and solve the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, vilifying any group is not a good idea and we should very consciously try to avoid this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a problem that has emerged and we have observed in other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is one lesson that we are taking away.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Do not go around vilifying various groups and saying that you should have done this, you should have done that.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is better to preserve the relationship and find ways to work together.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, in this context, I was listening carefully to Members' contributions and I appreciate all of them a great deal.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I could not help but notice that, amongst the Members who spoke from the Workers' Party, there was this term that was repeated quite a few times.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is what Mr Vikram Nair also responded to.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He said that he disagreed with this idea that there is a crisis of confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am not sure what the purpose of describing this problem this way is.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We do have a situation that we are dealing with and we are taking it very seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But let me perhaps offer a viewpoint from the agencies and the officers who are looking at this problem and listening to this debate and share what it comes across like to them.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a bit like, you know, firefighters on the frontline.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: You are trying all ways and means to, firstly, figure out what is the terrain that you are working with and trying to push back the fire, not let it spread.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And there, we have a group of bystanders who are, you know, instead of praying for them, encouraging them, we are saying to them: you should be doing this, you should be doing that – pontificating.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And then, when they do manage to put out some fires, with great effort and actually getting ready to fight the next fire because they know it is coming, the very same bystanders say, "Thank goodness, I said that." You know, see, how wonderful!

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a tough fight and I think our agencies and all the people involved they are not just public officers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By all means recognise the fact that there are also private sector players involved.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And I think one of the Members said it is quite thankless.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I believe it was Ms Hany Soh who said so and I appreciate her for acknowledging that.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, Sir, overall, I am still very glad that all parties support the Motion and have largely avoided grandstanding.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I call on Members to please use your own networks and your social media influence not to spread this, you know, very easy labels, to tag onto something like this, but to spread awareness of the tools that can really help people.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I think that is a far better use of your social media influence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And my humble appeal to all Members who have contributed your ideas and suggestions, please give our agencies time to consider the feedback and to prioritise what is most needle-moving, because, actually, it will not be a matter of doing more, but doing more of the right things continuously.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At any one time, we will be introducing new measures while designing some more.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, I would like to announce three today.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Standard will set out best practices that reduce the risk of malicious actors exploiting weaknesses in the app design.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, apps could be designed to require additional authentication of a user before authorising high-risk transactions, such as those providing access to our assets or savings.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Standard will also recommend that developers build in malware detection capabilities on their apps, since this feature has proven to be effective in disrupting scammers' unauthorised transactions using compromised devices.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: CSA will incorporate more of such effective practices in the Standard as they emerge or as the technologies evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: CSA will also consider how best to help end-users easily identify apps that meet these Standards.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the Standard is new, we will assess its usefulness in due course and whether to keep it voluntary or make it mandatory.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides apps that people use, we must also better protect vulnerable segments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It calls for measures to help frontline staff identify vulnerable consumers during service sign-up and handle cases of suspected exploitation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Guidelines also encourage telcos to waive charges for vulnerable consumers who have fallen victim to scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Arising from earlier cases encountered, MHA is also exploring ways to better protect the public, particularly those who continue to believe the scammers, despite being warned by the Police and even their own family members.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the landscape evolves, we will need to grow new capabilities to keep pace with scammers and online risks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Several Members mentioned the misuse of deepfakes to create compelling pitches, such as the recent ads featuring our leaders' likeness to promote crypto scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These research efforts will also help inform new legislation or regulations that we will need for issues, such as deepfakes, and which we are studying.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Ms Tan pointed out, even with extensive efforts by the Government and businesses, we must each do our part as individuals to remain vigilant online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, we should adopt measures that can mitigate the risks of scams, even if they may seem inconvenient or unnecessarily strict.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This could mean downloading and enabling the ScamShield app or turning on multi-factor authentication for online services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We should avoid downloading apps from unfamiliar sources and avoid responding to suspicious videos promising guaranteed returns on investments or giveaways.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When accessing websites, individuals should also exercise vigilance by always checking the URL in the address bar of their web browser.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We agree with Mr Ong that consumer banking and messaging service providers can do more to prompt users to adopt such habits.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government will continue working with key industry players to further strengthen efforts to raise public awareness.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, we should educate ourselves on the latest scam trends and anti-scam measures such as those on ScamAlert.sg.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even as we continue our efforts to stop scams and recover losses, we must not forget about the trauma experienced by victims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Anti-Scam Resource Guide on SPF's website also sets out additional avenues of community support.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Sharael Taha suggested reviewing the process of freezing bank accounts for the entire duration of the investigation period.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The time taken for investigations can differ from case to case.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Victims with frozen bank accounts may be offered new ones by banks, which may come with restricted access to certain facilities, or be subject to enhanced monitoring measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But these will still meet basic banking needs such as receiving salaries and Government support.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If not, I would suggest that the Leader of the House moves —

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, firstly, I would like to reiterate my support for the Motion put forward by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singapore's digital journey has brought great benefits, such as new economic opportunities for our people and businesses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, it has also introduced new risks, including digitally-enabled scams that many people are concerned about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, the Government must enable our people to ride the wave of opportunities arising from our digital transformation, whilst doing everything possible to strengthen safety and trust in our digital domain.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To this end, the Government has prioritised efforts to deal with scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many measures have been implemented and proven to be effective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, as the scammers evolve their tactics, we too must update our counter measures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is no silver bullet in the fight against scams; neither can the Government do it alone.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a long-term battle that requires everyone's cooperation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I believe that with persistent efforts and contributions from everyone, the battle can eventually be won.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And you still have 30 seconds to spare.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First of all, I would like to state categorically that in my speech, I did not do so to politicise the issue or to create panic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My desire was to actually reflect what I see as the current sentiment in significant sections of the public.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That is almost 100% of the people in this age group who are worried about becoming scam victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, messages to enrol in Healthier SG are ignored.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Third, I think we all know the statistics of scam losses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the Minister herself pointed out, the fact that there is so much public education now, may also lead to feelings of anxiety in the public, which I think are very real.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, I myself have received feedback from members of the public who expressed the desire to take their accounts offline.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These could include retirees, with their CPF transactions and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not think they are isolated incidents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would argue that there is a serious issue with public confidence and I think it is borne out by these factors that I have mentioned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And I also acknowledged the work done by the agencies – it is not that we are ignorant of such.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, we do appreciate it and realise that it is a big task and a 24/7 effort.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, Mr Speaker, I would argue that I believe I am entitled to my opinion, just as the Minister is entitled her opinion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I do not think there is a question that we are each entitled to our opinions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was not a question of opinion at all.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is simply to say that following the debate, whatever goes on to social media for the benefit of the people who are not able to take part in this discussion, I hope that messages being put out by MPs do not simply use very sensational, glaring headlines.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would very much appreciate if we can keep our efforts focused on the actual things that will make a difference.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I appreciate that if there is alignment on this issue across the aisle.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I would also urge MPs – let us try to keep it that way.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is the only way we can win this war against the scammers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, we have heard views approaching this topic from many different angles.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my capacity as Deputy Chairman of the GPCs for Culture, Community and Youth and Education, I would like to focus on the issue of online harms and the impact of online harms on two specific groups in our community – women and children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And also from an education perspective, what more can be done to help mitigate the impact of online harms through education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although there has yet to be a universally accepted definition of what constitute online harms, this can be broadly described as online behaviour that may directly or indirectly hurt a person physically or emotionally, harmful information that is posted online or information sent to a person via electronic means.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Increasingly, countries are realising the dangers of online harms and the adverse impacts they could have on vulnerable communities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The UK passed the Online Safety Bill in October 2023 to protect people, especially children, from online harms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these codes of conducts and regulations were introduced and passed in good faith and they are laudable and much needed attempts to make online spaces safer, they are also broad strokes that probably do not adequately capture the complexities of online harms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Online harms are notoriously nebulous and regulating them is difficult because, although they are undesirable and morally questionable, many of them are not, strictly speaking, illegal.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, how do we define and regulate trolling, cancel campaigns and the issue of body shaming online?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Different people would understand and interpret them somewhat differently, depending on whether they are engaging those activities or are on the receiving end of such behaviours.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These online behaviours, although not illegal, can cause severe mental distress, emotional anguish and diminish the self-worth of victims, even causing victims to experience physical harm if left unchecked over prolonged period.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe there is an urgent need to tackle these non-illegal but distressful online harms since they are more likely to happen on a day-to-day basis on social media platforms, thereby impacting a wider community, and are harder to detect and act on than overt online dangers such as terrorism propaganda, child sexual abuse and other exploitation materials.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Overt online danger such as terrorism propaganda, sexual exploitation and abuse, threats to racial and religious harmony and public health are entirely different from online harms such as cyberstalking, body shaming, unwanted sexual attention, trolling and cancel campaigns.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, bundling them together within the same topology of undesirable online content could sometimes risk obfuscating the nature and impact of these online harms, potentially reducing the efficacy of remedy or remedial actions that can be undertaken.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe there is a need for us to adopt a similar approach to classify online harms in Singapore in a more nuanced manner, so that we can build a more robust regulatory framework on online harms, implement target-based upstream preventive education in schools and communities to inoculate as we educate Singaporeans, especially women and children, against online harms and provide victim-centric downstream remediation support by working with civil societies and other groups to offer accessible legal and non-legal assistance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Worryingly, there are also youths who believe that women who upload images online should be accepting of negative comments; as in, it is acceptable to receive sexually explicit images even when unrequested.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The results from the two studies are telling.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, they suggest that the actual number of victims of online harms might be higher than we think because many victims are unwilling to come forward to disclose their experience because they feel that disclosure and reporting would not make much difference to their ordeals.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, the results also suggest that not only is there a general lack of awareness about such harms, but there is also a certain level of apathy among youths on the possible repercussions arising from these harms, ironically when they themselves are more likely to be the target of such behaviours.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Extending this line of argument further, the lack of awareness and being apathetic towards online harms might result in youths becoming unintentional perpetrators of such behaviours.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as how some companies require their employees to complete annual mandatory e-learning exercises and quizzes on the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), for example, perhaps all students in Singapore above a certain age must complete the module and obtain a minimum score in the online harms quiz.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, I hope that we can take a more strident position on perpetrators of online harms, bearing in mind the long-term scarring impact that such harms might have on victims.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, at present, I believe there is only one dedicated centre – SG Her Empowerment – where victims of online harms can seek assistance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Government consider working with other civil society groups, especially community-based ones, to provide additional avenues for victims of online harms to seek for assistance?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe making these statistics and the identification even of convicted perpetrators available will give victims the assurance that their voices are being heard and actions will be taken to safeguard their online safety.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We began to take a serious view on misinformation and disinformation in 2017 when we conducted a review on our existing laws to combat fake news.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With generative AI and deepfakes opening up a new frontier on online harms, I believe that it is timely that we calibrate our approach towards online harms by taking a more serious view on them and thereby making a digital indeed, not just inclusive, but a safe space for our community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I end my speech in firm support of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It should be a clarification and not a speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I just have one question for Minister Josephine Teo.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am glad that many Members have pointed out that digital inclusivity is also about ensuring that digital systems are inclusive and user-friendly and not deployed just for profit-seeking by businesses.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That indeed is PSP's core position as presented by my colleague, Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that will be more appropriate, so that a proper response can be given.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Past Parliament Sittings have seen colleagues from both sides of the aisle raising questions and putting forth suggestions on different issues pertaining to both opportunities and risks that come with digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I am heartened that we have had a robust debate on this Motion in this House today and most of all, I am heartened by the echos of support for the Motion, from both sides of the aisle, that the GPC for Communications and Information has put forth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And I sincerely appreciate the interest and support from the Workers' Party, namely, Ms Sylvia Lim, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Gerald Giam as well as the Progress Singapore Party, Ms Hazel Poa and, of course, our Nominated Members of Parliament (NMPs), Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim, Mr Ong Hua Han, Ms Usha Chandradas, Mr Mark Lee and Ms Jean See, in this Moton debate as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I will not recap everyone's points and suggestions, but I have gained useful insights from all of you in this House.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Through the debate, it is clear that Singapore is not alone in facing the challenges that come along with digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Challenges, such as scams and online harms, have been a global issue.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Advanced economies, like the US, UK and Europe are also still in the process of better understanding the issues and formulating responses and safeguards to better protect their own citizens, given the evolving nature of these risks and challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given the many initiatives implemented at different points of time, some publicised and some not, it is sometimes easy to misunderstand the Government as being too slow, too slacked, uncaring and only favouring business or money.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But arising from this debate, I am glad to note the suite of Government initiatives in place to detect, deter and protect Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The "big picture" is a lot clearer now.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ultimately, both sides of this House do not disagree that digitalisation has and will continue to bring benefits to our nation and our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But there are risks that we must manage and we will, because it is debilitating if we stop moving forward and living our lives, just because we are worried about all the possible consequences outside.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I should add that we need to also recognise that there is always a balance to be struck.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, let us also be mindful that there will be trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Still, it remains that we all need to do more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If everyone is willing to take on a larger share of the responsibility, we can protect more people and reduce the possible harms to the ordinary citizen.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Earlier on, I mentioned the opportunities and challenges brought forth by digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Online harm is also evolving rapidly, as the Chinese saying goes "the higher the level, the greater the devil".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope that through the combined efforts of the Government, businesses and the people, we can defeat the devils even as they get more sophisticated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thus, we will be able to build an inclusive and safe digital society with deep trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): As I conclude, I would like to echo what my fellow Parliamentary colleagues have expounded in this debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With stronger partnerships between the Government, industry players and our people, Singapore can be the beacon and lead the world in fostering trust in the digital future, through a safe and inclusive digital society.
